claim: Policy of Oct 2022: acquisitions of control of Canadian critical-minerals businesses by foreign state-owned or state-influenced enterprises approved only on an exceptional basis; it is not Korea-specific and no source found applying it to Korean firms.

name: Canada steel tariff-rate quotas and surtax; Korean complaint
institution: Department of Finance Canada / Korea MOTIR
claim: From 26 Dec 2025 Canada cut FTA-partner steel quotas to 75% of 2024 volumes with a 50% over-quota surtax; Korea protested that this breaches the CKFTA and sought an exemption, none found; whether non-oriented electrical steel is covered is not confirmed.

name: Canada submarine programme: TKMS selected over Hanwha Ocean (KSS-III)
source: Korea JoongAng Daily; Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada
claim: Carney named Germany's TKMS preferred supplier for up to 12 submarines on 6 Jul 2026 (NATO interoperability cited); contracting runs through 2027 and Canada kept the option to open talks with Hanwha Ocean if TKMS talks fail.

name: Hanwha Ocean industrial-benefit offers tied to Canadian steel and technology
claim: Hanwha's bid carried MOUs on steel, satellite communications, AI, space and sensors plus Canadian steel use and technology transfer; the article does not link the bid to energy, critical minerals or batteries; offers lapse unless Canada reopens talks.

name: Carney-Lee meeting at G7 (Evian) on defence, energy and critical minerals
institution: Prime Minister's Office Canada / Korea Presidential Office
claim: Lee and Carney agreed on 16 Jun 2026 to strengthen cooperation in defence, security, energy and critical minerals; an informal meeting followed at the NATO summit; no deliverables or amounts reported.

name: POSCO Future M-GM Ultium CAM cathode plant, Becancour (Quebec)
claim: JV owned 85% by POSCO Future M and 15% by GM; phase 1 (20,000 t/yr high-nickel cathode, all for Ultium Cells) was scheduled for late Oct 2026 after earlier delays; phase 2 timing unconfirmed; no source found confirming start-up has occurred.

name: EcoPro BM-SK On-Ford cathode plant, Becancour (Quebec)
source: S&P Global Mobility; Korean press (via search summary)
claim: C$1.2bn, 45,000 t/yr plant (originally 1H 2026) was halted twice in 2024 and resumed in Sep 2024; one undated Korean report says Ford is leaving; current status and ownership not confirmed in any 2026 source; USD figure is the 2023 announcement value.

name: NextStar Energy cell plant, Windsor (LGES-Stellantis)
claim: Series cell production began Nov 2025 and the plant was officially opened in Mar 2026, initially focused on stationary storage; employment 1,300+ against a 2,500 target.

name: LG Energy Solution buys Stellantis 49% stake in NextStar Energy
claim: LGES agreed in early Feb 2026 to take full ownership of NextStar by buying Stellantis's 49%, with Stellantis staying a customer; closing subject to approvals and not confirmed; publication day approximate.

name: LGES supply MOUs with Electra, Avalon and Snow Lake (cobalt sulphate, lithium hydroxide)
claim: In 2022 LGES signed non-binding MOUs for 7,000 t of cobalt sulphate over three years from 2023 and 55,000 t of lithium hydroxide over five years from 2025; signing date inferred from the Sep 2022 Toronto visit; later delivery not confirmed.

name: Hydro Lithium 10-year offtake of Prairie Lithium Phase 1 output (Saskatchewan brine)
source: Prairie Lithium ASX announcement (via search summary)
claim: Binding agreement for 100% of Phase 1 (about 150 t/yr LCE) for ten years, renewable to 30; crystallite reported to be refined in Korea, first production targeted Q4 2026; sources differ on whether Hydro Lithium is Korean-based.

name: Samsung SDI US$18.5m investment in Canada Nickel (Crawford project option)
claim: Samsung SDI bought 15.6m Canada Nickel shares for US$18.5m with an option on 10% of the Crawford nickel-cobalt sulphide project carrying offtake rights; date not shown in the source.

name: KHNP-ARC-NB Power ARC-100 SMR at Point Lepreau (New Brunswick)
institution: Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power / ARC Clean Technology / NB Power
source: Korea Times; NEI Magazine (via search summary)
claim: Non-binding KHNP, ARC and NB Power agreements (MOU Nov 2023, trilateral May 2024, Dec 2024 partnership) for the ARC-100 SMR targeting commissioning around 2030; no 2025-26 update found; publication day approximate.

name: Reported 10-year Cameco uranium supply deal with KHNP
claim: One trade report describes a 10-year Cameco supply deal with KHNP but gives no date, and no Cameco or KHNP release was found; KHNP's confirmed 2025 enrichment deal is with US-based Centrus.

name: Cameco backs Westinghouse settlement with KEPCO and KHNP
claim: Cameco publicly supported the Jan 2025 resolution of Westinghouse's IP dispute with KEPCO and KHNP, calling it a framework for further reactor deployments; a link to Canadian uranium or conversion supply is not stated.

name: Coverage gap: no Korea-Canada deals found for NGO steel, power cables or aluminium wire rod
claim: Searches found no Korean-Canadian investment, offtake or supply deal in non-oriented electrical steel, power cables or aluminium wire rod; the Jan 2026 MOU names only automotive, batteries, critical minerals and AI.

name: United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA/CUSMA)
claim: USMCA entered into force on 1 Jul 2020; under Article 34.7.1 it terminates on 1 Jul 2036 unless each Party confirms it wishes to continue for a new 16-year term.

name: First USMCA joint review (1 Jul 2026): no US extension; annual reviews from 2027
source: Federal Register 2026-20341 (USTR); Global Affairs Canada Canada-US engagement page
claim: The Free Trade Commission held the first joint review on 1 Jul 2026 and the United States did not agree to extend the agreement for a new 16-year term, so the Commission must review it annually until all three Parties confirm extension or the term expires. USTR opened comments for the 2027 annual review on 5 Oct 2026 (deadline 12 Jan 2027), inviting views on North American economic security and non-market practices.

name: IEEPA tariffs on Canadian goods (from 4 Mar 2025) ended by the Supreme Court ruling
source: CBP IEEPA FAQ (modified 2026-04-14); CBP trade remedies page
claim: IEEPA duties applied to Canadian goods entered from 4 Mar 2025, with USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from 7 Mar 2025 and energy products at an additional 10%; after the Supreme Court's 20 Feb 2026 ruling (see E08) CBP launched the CAPE refund tool in ACE on 20 Apr 2026. The later 35% rate on non-USMCA goods is not stated in the CBP source.

name: Section 301 forced-labour tariff on Canada (10%), USMCA duty-free goods exempt
claim: USTR found that Canada failed to effectively enforce its forced-labour import prohibition and imposed a 10% Section 301 tariff on Canadian products from 24 Jul 2026 (Mexico gets the same rate). Products of Canada entered duty-free under USMCA are exempt, as are goods under Section 232 auto-parts, medium/heavy-duty vehicle and semiconductor headings.

name: Section 338 duties on Canada over its motor-vehicle countermeasures (Proclamation 11048)
claim: Invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the President found Canada's surtax on US vehicles (25% on non-USMCA vehicles and on non-Canadian/Mexican content of USMCA vehicles, plus company-specific quotas) discriminatory and imposed a 50% additional duty on certain Canadian products listed in an annex, effective 19 Aug 2026. The proclamation says US vehicle exports to Canada fell about 22% (US$25.9bn to US$20.3bn) between Apr 2025 and Mar 2026 versus a year earlier.

name: Section 338 duties on Canada over dairy TRQ eligibility (Proclamation 11047)
claim: The President found that Canada lets retailers use its CETA cheese tariff-rate quota but not its USMCA one, and imposed a 50% additional duty on certain Canadian products under Section 338 from 19 Aug 2026.

name: Section 338 duties on Canada over provincial bans on US alcohol (Proclamation 11046)
claim: All provinces and territories halted sales of US alcohol from March 2025 (only Alberta and Saskatchewan lifted bans, in June 2025); the proclamation says US alcohol exports to Canada fell about 81% (US$718m to US$137m) and imposed a 50% Section 338 duty on certain Canadian products from 19 Aug 2026.

name: Section 338 import bans on certain Canadian products (Proclamations 11061-11063)
claim: The 50% duties were suspended for three days (Proclamation 11056) after Canada committed to remove the measures; the US states Canada reneged and ceased negotiating on 21 Aug 2026, so the duties took effect on 22 Aug. Proclamation 11063 bans imports of certain Canadian products from 29 Sep 2026 (the product annex is not in the text version), and parallel exclusion proclamations for the dairy and alcohol cases were published the same day.

name: Section 338 motor-vehicle duties re-scoped and stacked on Section 232 (Proclamation 11076)
claim: From 30 Oct 2026 some Canadian products leave and others join the 50% Section 338 duty list (after an earlier rescoping on 8 Sep 2026), and the duties now apply in addition to Section 232 duties; the July proclamation had excluded Section 232 articles.

name: Canadian counter-tariffs on US steel, aluminium and autos
source: Department of Finance Canada, Canada's response to US tariffs (archived page dated 2026-06-19)
claim: Canada keeps 25% counter-tariffs on US steel and aluminium (part of the 13 Mar 2025 C$29.8bn package, including C$12.6bn steel and C$3bn aluminium) and, from 9 Apr 2025, on non-CUSMA US vehicles and the non-Canadian/Mexican content of CUSMA vehicles, with an automaker remission framework tied to Canadian production. 25% tariffs on C$44.2bn of other US goods were removed on 1 Sep 2025.

name: Section 232 steel, aluminium and copper tariffs as applied to Canada (Proclamations 11021 and 11032)
claim: Proclamation 11021 (2 Apr 2026) set full-value Section 232 duties of 50% on steel, aluminium and certain copper articles, with lower UK rates only. For the Annex I-C derivative list, Proclamation 11032 charges USMCA-qualifying Canadian and Mexican products 25% on non-US content only (floor 15%), while Japan, Korea, the EU, the UK and others receive a 15% all-in cap that Canada does not.

name: Section 232 autos, auto parts and medium/heavy-duty vehicles: USMCA content rules for Canada
source: CBP trade remedies page (Section 232 autos and MHDV listings)
claim: Section 232 duties on autos and parts (from Apr 2025) and on medium/heavy-duty vehicles and buses (Proclamation 10984 of 17 Oct 2025) continue, with a 2 Feb 2026 procedure for US-content submissions, 6 May 2026 guidance on USMCA-qualifying trucks and a 29 Jun 2026 duty-offset notice for parts. The rates for Canadian vehicles are not stated on the CBP page.

name: Section 232 softwood timber and lumber tariff (10%) and deferred wood-product increases
claim: A 10% Section 232 tariff on certain softwood timber and lumber has applied since 14 Oct 2025, on top of other duties. Proclamation 11000 deferred the rise for upholstered furniture (25% to 30%) and kitchen cabinets and vanities (25% to 50%) to 1 Jan 2027, except for countries that reach an agreement; it names no Canadian exemption.

name: Canada-US Joint Action Plan on Critical Minerals Collaboration
claim: Announced on 9 Jan 2020 after a June 2019 leaders' commitment, the plan covers industry engagement, supply chains for strategic industries and defence, sharing information on mineral resources, cooperation in multilateral forums, joint R&D and supply-chain modelling. The release names no funding, targets or review dates, and its current status is not stated in any 2025-26 source.

name: G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan (Kananaskis, Canada's G7 presidency)
source: Prime Minister of Canada, G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan
claim: G7 leaders adopted the plan at Kananaskis on 17 Jun 2025, under Canada's presidency. It tasks ministers with a roadmap for standards-based markets with traceability by year-end, calls on export credit agencies, DFIs and MDBs to scale up mining finance, and targets processing, recycling and substitution R&D. Australia, India and Korea later endorsed it.

name: Critical Minerals Production Alliance (Canada-led, G7)
institution: Natural Resources Canada / G7 energy and environment ministers
source: Budget 2025 (Finance Canada), chapter 1; G7 Energy and Environment Ministers' Chairs' Summary, Toronto, 31 Oct 2025 (G7 Research Group copy)
claim: Carney launched the Alliance at Kananaskis to use strategic investments and offtakes to bring critical-mineral projects into production for defence and advanced technology. At the 30-31 Oct 2025 Toronto ministerial, ministers agreed their critical-minerals envoys would advance the work, and Canada announced investments including offtakes with two Canadian projects. Member list, deal count, values and the US role are not stated in either source.

name: G7 Roadmap to Promote Standards-based Markets for Critical Minerals
source: G7 Research Group (copy of the Toronto ministerial annex)
claim: Adopted in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025 as an early action under the Action Plan, it aims to reduce and eventually eliminate dependence on supply chains dominated by non-market practices. It prioritises interoperable traceability systems aligned with the UN Transparency Protocol and lists price floors, procurement, tax and trade measures as tools members may use, with no deadlines.

name: Canada Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund (C$2bn) and First and Last Mile Fund
claim: Budget 2025 proposes C$2bn over five years from 2026-27 (about US$1.44bn at 0.72 USD/CAD) for a Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund making equity investments, loan guarantees and offtakes, plus C$371.8m for a First and Last Mile Fund that absorbs the Critical Minerals Infrastructure Fund for up to C$1.5bn through 2029-30. The Budget frames these as a response to the US remaking its trade relationships; they are Canadian instruments, not bilateral ones.

name: Fireweed Metals Mactung tungsten: DoD DPA Title III award with Canadian CMIF co-funding
institution: US DoD (DPA Title III) / Natural Resources Canada (CMIF)
source: Fireweed Metals news release; Fireweed news page
claim: On 13 Dec 2024 the US DoD awarded US$15.8m under DPA Title III to take the Yukon Mactung tungsten project toward a final investment decision, and Canada's CMIF offered up to C$12.9m for road and power planning (C$35.4m combined; the CMIF agreement was signed 27 Aug 2025). A feasibility study began on 9 Mar 2026, and JX Advanced Metals took a strategic stake in a C$61.5m placement closed on 2 Apr 2026.

name: Electra cobalt sulfate refinery (Ontario): DoD DPA Title III award
institution: Electra Battery Materials / US DoD / Government of Canada / Ontario
source: Electra news releases (19 Aug 2024 DoD award; Q3 2026 results)
claim: The DoD awarded US$20m under DPA Title III on 19 Aug 2024, noting Canada's eligibility for Title III funds. As of 9 Nov 2026 the ~C$100m (US$73m) build is on budget with C$59.3m of government contributions (including a C$20m federal agreement of 4 May 2026 and C$17.5m from Ontario); early commissioning is targeted for Q4 2026 and commercial production for 2H 2027, at 5,120 t/yr contained cobalt, with about 60% committed to LG Energy Solution.

name: Ucore rare-earth separation: DoD awards for the Louisiana SMC and Canadian funding
institution: Ucore Rare Metals / US DoD (DoW) / Natural Resources Canada
claim: Canadian-listed Ucore executed a US$18.4m DoD award in May 2025 for its Louisiana Strategic Metals Complex and got another US$4.6m from the Department of War on 14 Sep 2026 for samarium and gadolinium refining (US$23.0m total); Canada gave conditional approval for up to C$36.3m on 29 Oct 2025. It shipped NdPr oxide qualification samples in Jun 2026 and received initial commissioning feedstock in Louisiana on 9 Nov 2026.

name: Saskatchewan Research Council-REalloys rare-earth metal offtake and heavy-rare-earth metallization partnership
institution: Saskatchewan Research Council / Government of Saskatchewan / REalloys
claim: Under a five-year offtake signed 8 Dec 2025, REalloys will buy most of the NdPr metal and Dy/Tb oxide output of SRC's Saskatoon facility (400 t/yr NdPr metal rising to 600 t/yr; full operation expected early 2027) for US defence clients. On 12 Mar 2026 REalloys announced a heavy-rare-earth metallization facility to be built in Saskatoon and later moved to Ohio, taking 80% of the output.

name: Coverage gap: no US offtaker or US public finance at Nouveau Monde Graphite
institution: Nouveau Monde Graphite / Canada Growth Fund
source: NMG Q3 2026 update; Canada Growth Fund news page
claim: The Matawinie mine has been under construction since 2026 (C$67m spent by 30 Sep 2026; mining lease granted Oct 2026), and the 13 ktpy Becancour anode plant is targeting FID in the coming months. Offtakers for about 70% of output are Panasonic Energy, Traxys and the Government of Canada, and the Canada Growth Fund committed about US$82m in Apr 2026; no US buyer or US government finance is named.

name: DOE conditional commitment of up to US$17.5bn for Westinghouse AP1000 long-lead items
institution: US DOE Office of Energy Dominance Financing / Westinghouse (Brookfield, Cameco)
claim: On 23 Jun 2026 DOE conditionally committed loans of up to US$17.5bn to fund long-lead items for up to 10 US AP1000 reactors through a Westinghouse SPV and up to five two-reactor project vehicles, each needing about $1bn of equity from Westinghouse and a partner. Definitive agreements are pending; Westinghouse is owned by Canada's Brookfield and Cameco, and the Oct 2025 partnership with the US Commerce Department (E28) is negotiated separately.

name: Darlington New Nuclear Project: first GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 SMR
institution: Ontario Power Generation / Canada Growth Fund / Building Ontario Fund / GE Vernova Hitachi
source: OPG Darlington SMR project page (update of 10 Nov 2026)
claim: The CNSC licensed construction on 4 Apr 2025, Ontario approved unit 1 on 8 May 2025, and Canada Growth Fund and Building Ontario Fund equity was agreed on 23 Oct 2025; the unit 1 basemat was placed in Apr 2026. On 10 Nov 2026 OPG said unit 1 will miss its Oct 2030 operation target and budget, with a new schedule and budget expected by mid-2027 with the reactor's US-based technology provider, GE Vernova Hitachi.

name: Champlain Hudson Power Express (Quebec-New York City HVDC line)
source: Office of the Governor of New York; CHPE project site
claim: Completion of the 339-mile, 1,250 MW buried HVDC line was announced on 16 Jun 2026; it can supply up to 20% of New York City's needs (about 10.4 TWh/yr) under a 25-year contract. The project site says the Hydro-Quebec contract with the State began on 1 June and the line is in full service.

name: Canada is the largest foreign energy supplier to the United States
source: Global Affairs Canada, Canada-US engagement (modified 2026-08-27); EIA Oil imports and exports explainer (updated 2024-01-19)
claim: Global Affairs Canada says the US is Canada's largest trading partner and Canada is its largest foreign energy supplier, and that the CUSMA review would consider digital trade, AI and energy stability. EIA's latest data on its explainer shows Canada supplied 60% of US gross crude imports and 52% of total petroleum imports in 2022.

name: Honda Alliston investment for hybrid production (EV value chain not mentioned)
claim: On 9 Nov 2026 Honda committed C$166m of capital spending (about US$119.5m at 0.72 USD/CAD), within a C$867m total, to retool Alliston, Ontario for hybrid and petrol models and resume engine making, with North America as the main market; Ontario's premier cited US tariffs. The release does not mention the C$15bn Ontario EV and battery value chain announced in 2024.

name: US additional 25% tariff on India over Russian oil (EO 14329)
source: Federal Register 2025-15267 and 2026-02818 (EO 14384); CNBC (6 Aug 2025) for the 50% total
claim: EO 14329, signed 6 Aug 2025, added a 25% ad valorem duty on goods of India because India imported Russian oil; it applied from 27 Aug 2025 and lifted the combined US tariff on many Indian goods to 50% with the 25% reciprocal rate. EO 14384 terminated it from 7 Feb 2026.

name: Removal of the Russian-oil tariff with monitoring and snapback (EO 14384)
claim: From 12:01 a.m. EST on 7 Feb 2026 products of India are no longer subject to the 25% Russian-oil duty and HTS headings 9903.01.84-89 are terminated. Commerce, with State and Treasury, monitors whether India resumes direct or indirect imports of Russian oil and may recommend reimposing the 25% duty.

name: US reciprocal tariff on India: 25% cut to 18%, then voided by the Supreme Court
source: White House fact sheet (9 Feb 2026); Wikipedia summary of Learning Resources v. Trump
claim: The White House said on 9 Feb 2026 that the IEEPA reciprocal tariff on India would fall from 25% to 18% under the trade framework. On 20 Feb 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, so the 18% rate lapsed and IEEPA duties became refundable (about US$81bn refunded to all importers by July 2026).

name: Section 122 temporary 10% import surcharge applied to Indian goods
source: Wikipedia (Learning Resources v. Trump; Tariffs in the second Trump administration), citing NBC News, BBC and NYT
claim: After the ruling a 10% Section 122 surcharge applied to Indian and almost all other imports from 24 Feb 2026 for 150 days. The Court of International Trade found it unjustified on 7 May 2026 (relief limited to the plaintiffs and stayed by the Federal Circuit in June 2026), and it expired on 24 Jul 2026.

name: Section 301 forced-labour tariff on India (10% band)
source: USTR press release (23 Jul 2026); BBC (24 Jul 2026)
claim: USTR took final Section 301 action on 60 economies on 23 Jul 2026. India is one of 17 economies at 10% (those with, or committed to, a forced-labour import ban) rather than the 12.5% default. Exemptions cover scarce raw materials and products whose tariffing would disrupt the economy. The duties replaced the Section 122 surcharge from 24 Jul 2026.

name: US-India Joint Statement: framework for an Interim Agreement (6 Feb 2026)
institution: White House / Ministry of Commerce and Industry
source: White House joint statement (6 Feb 2026); USTR statement
claim: India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on all US industrial goods and many farm goods. The US set an 18% reciprocal rate and, once the Interim Agreement is concluded, will remove it on generic pharmaceuticals, gems and aircraft parts, lift Section 232 tariffs on certain aircraft parts and give India a preferential quota for auto parts. Both sides agreed to align on economic security, including inbound and outbound investment reviews and export controls, and either side may modify its commitments if the other's tariffs change.

name: India's intended US$500bn purchase of US energy, aircraft, technology and coking coal
claim: India intends to purchase US$500bn of US energy products, aircraft and parts, precious metals, technology products and coking coal over five years, and trade in GPUs and other data-centre goods is to rise significantly. No annual schedule or enforcement mechanism is stated.

name: Mission 500 and launch of Bilateral Trade Agreement negotiations (13 Feb 2025)
source: White House US-India joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025)
claim: Leaders set Mission 500 to more than double bilateral trade to US$500bn by 2030 and planned to negotiate the first tranche of a multi-sector BTA by fall 2025. That deadline passed without a signed tranche.

name: US-India Interim Agreement still unconcluded (Oct 2026)
institution: USTR / Ministry of Commerce and Industry
claim: USTR Greer travelled to New Delhi in June 2026 to discuss the Joint Statement and the Interim Agreement. By late October 2026 no deal had been concluded; India's foreign ministry said both sides reaffirmed their commitment to concluding one, and a former Indian ambassador said India was waiting for the US to formalise its tariff positions.

name: US-India merchandise trade, April-September 2026
source: BBC (23 Oct 2026), citing India's commerce ministry
claim: India's merchandise exports to the US were US$50.81bn in April-September 2026, up 11.1% year on year, and imports from the US rose to US$32.33bn from US$25.66bn, narrowing India's surplus to US$18.48bn.

name: India's purchases of Russian crude
claim: India took 37% of Russia's crude oil exports between December 2022 and July 2026. The US withdrew its Russian-oil penalty in February 2026 but the purchases remain an irritant, and in October 2026 the US temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel.

name: Rubio energy-focused visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar (Oct 2026)
claim: Secretary Rubio's second India visit of 2026 focused on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties: he met Jaishankar in Mumbai, toured Reliance's 1.4m b/d Jamnagar refinery and urged more refining of Venezuelan crude. No purchase commitments were announced.

name: Proposed Brownsville, Texas refinery linked to Reliance
claim: Trump announced a proposed refinery at the Port of Brownsville, Texas, in March 2026, and analysts said Rubio sought assurance in October 2026 that Reliance remained interested in backing it. Reliance has not commented publicly and no project details or timeline are published.

name: Pending US bill authorising 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian oil and gas
claim: In September 2026 the House voted to advance a bill authorising 100% tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas, which would cover India, while extending Iran sanctions. Enactment status is not stated in the source.

name: US-India COMPACT for the 21st Century (13 Feb 2025)
source: White House US-India joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025)
claim: Leaders launched the COMPACT (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology) as the umbrella for defence, trade, energy and technology outcomes, and welcomed about US$7.35bn of ongoing Indian investment in the US, including Novelis aluminium in Alabama and Kentucky, JSW steel in Texas and Ohio and Epsilon Advanced Materials battery materials in North Carolina.

name: Epsilon Advanced Materials battery-materials investment in North Carolina
source: White House US-India joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025)
claim: The February 2025 leaders' statement lists Epsilon Advanced Materials' manufacture of critical battery materials in North Carolina among ongoing Indian investments in the US. The plant is reported elsewhere as a synthetic-graphite anode facility; its value and construction status are not stated in the source.

name: US-India TRUST initiative and Strategic Mineral Recovery initiative
source: White House US-India joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025)
claim: TRUST (Transforming the Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology) covers AI, semiconductors, quantum, biotech, energy and space and commits to trusted supply chains for semiconductors and critical minerals. Under it the leaders launched the Strategic Mineral Recovery initiative to recover and process lithium, cobalt and rare earths from aluminium, coal-mining and oil-and-gas streams; no budget or project list is given.

name: US-India initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET, 2023), predecessor of TRUST
source: White House fact sheet (31 Jan 2023, archived)
claim: The two National Security Advisors held the inaugural iCET meeting on 31 Jan 2023, covering semiconductor supply chains, AI, quantum, space and defence innovation, and named rare-earth processing and advanced materials for future cooperation. The February 2025 leaders' statement carries this agenda forward under TRUST and does not mention iCET.

name: US-India Energy Security Partnership (re-committed Feb 2025)
institution: DOE / Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
source: White House US-India joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025)
claim: Leaders re-committed to the Energy Security Partnership covering oil, gas and civil nuclear, aimed to make the US a leading supplier of crude, petroleum products and LNG to India, backed India's full IEA membership and agreed to expand strategic oil-reserve arrangements. The statement does not mention the earlier Strategic Clean Energy Partnership.

name: Minerals Security Partnership (India member since June 2023) and successor FORGE
institution: US State Department / Ministry of Mines
source: White House joint leaders' statement (13 Feb 2025); Wikipedia (MSP), citing ThePrint and State Department
claim: Both countries are MSP members (India joined in June 2023) and committed in February 2025 to promote investment along the critical-mineral value chain through it. The MSP was succeeded by FORGE at the February 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial; India's FORGE membership is not confirmed in the sources.

name: India joins Pax Silica (20 Feb 2026)
institution: US State Department / Government of India
source: Upstox news (20 Feb 2026), via Wikipedia (Pax Silica)
claim: India joined the US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI, semiconductor and critical-mineral supply chains on 20 Feb 2026, after being left out of the December 2025 launch group; the initiative now has about 27 signatories including the EU.

name: US countervailing and anti-dumping cases on solar cells and modules from India, Indonesia and Laos
technology: crystalline silicon solar cells and modules
source: Reuters (25 Feb 2026), via Wikipedia (Tariffs in the second Trump administration)
claim: In February 2026 Commerce set preliminary countervailing duties on solar cells and panels from India, Indonesia and Laos following a 2025 petition by US manufacturers. Company rates, the anti-dumping preliminaries and the final Commerce and ITC determinations are not stated in the source.

name: First Solar thin-film module plant in Tamil Nadu
claim: First Solar commissioned its Tamil Nadu module factory in 2024, its only plant in India, alongside US plants in Ohio, Alabama and Louisiana. Its capacity is reported at about 3.3 GW a year but is not stated in the source.

name: DFC loan for First Solar's India plant
claim: DFC committed debt financing of up to US$500m in 2023 to First Solar's Indian subsidiary for the Tamil Nadu module plant. The amount, date and disbursement status are not confirmed in the source.

name: DFC loan for Tata Power Solar cell and module plant (Tamil Nadu)
source: DFC active projects; CNBC-TV18 (17 Sep 2024) via Wikipedia (Tata Power)
claim: Tata Power built a 4.3 GW solar cell and module plant near Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, expected to be fully running by October 2024, and DFC is reported to have lent about US$425m for it in 2023. The loan amount and terms are not confirmed in the source.

name: Waaree Solar Americas module plant, Brookshire, Texas
claim: Waaree's US subsidiary runs a module plant in Brookshire, Texas, reported at 1.6 GW with production from about the turn of 2024-25, and has announced expansion to 3.2 GW and US cell production. Capacities, dates and any expansion progress are not confirmed in the source.

name: Vikram Solar evaluating a US manufacturing plant
source: Business Standard (26 Dec 2025); BusinessLine (26 Nov 2025), via Wikipedia
claim: Vikram Solar's chairman said in December 2025 the company was evaluating setting up manufacturing in the United States. It commissioned a 5 GW module plant at Vallam, Tamil Nadu, in November 2025 and listed in August 2025 after a Rs 2,079 crore (about US$236m) IPO; no US site or capacity has been announced.

name: India ALMM List-II for solar cells and basic customs duty on cells and modules
claim: India's Approved List of Models and Manufacturers extends to solar cells (List-II) from 1 June 2026 for government-backed, open-access and net-metered projects, on top of basic customs duty of about 25% on cells and 40% on modules (in place since April 2022). The order date and current duty split are not confirmed in the source.

name: India PLI scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries
source: Ministry of Heavy Industries scheme page
claim: Cabinet approved the ACC PLI on 12 May 2021 with Rs 18,100 crore (about US$2.06bn at Rs 88/US$). Beneficiaries must reach 25% domestic value addition rising to 60% within five years and invest Rs 225 crore per GWh; three firms hold 30 GWh, 20 GWh is open for fresh allocation, and the performance period runs 2025-2029.

name: India National Critical Mineral Mission
claim: Approved by Cabinet on 29 Jan 2025 with Rs 16,300 crore of central spending and an expected Rs 18,000 crore from public-sector companies to 2030-31 (about US$3.9bn in total at Rs 88/US$), covering exploration, overseas asset acquisition, processing parks and recycling. The figures are not confirmed in the source.

name: India scheme for sintered rare-earth permanent magnets
claim: Cabinet approved on 26 Nov 2025 a Rs 7,280 crore (about US$827m at Rs 88/US$) scheme to build 6,000 tonnes a year of integrated rare-earth permanent magnet capacity through competitively selected beneficiaries over seven years. The approval details and award status are not confirmed in the source.

name: KABIL lithium exploration blocks in Catamarca, Argentina
claim: KABIL signed an agreement with Catamarca's state miner CAMYEN on 15 Jan 2024 to explore and develop five lithium brine blocks (about 15,700 ha) for roughly Rs 200 crore (about US$23m at Rs 88/US$). Exploration results and the date and value are not confirmed in the source.

name: SHANTI Act 2025 opens Indian nuclear power to private and joint-venture operators
institution: Parliament of India / Department of Atomic Energy
source: PIB press note on the SHANTI Bill (19 Dec 2025); PIB parliament reply (23 Jul 2026); CSIS (19 Dec 2025)
claim: Enacted as Act No. 39 of 2025 (assent 20 Dec 2025), it repeals the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010, licenses private and joint-venture entities to build and operate plants, make equipment and fabricate some fuel, and keeps enrichment, heavy water and high-level waste with the central government. It sets graded operator liability of Rs 100-3,000 crore (about US$12-360m), limits supplier recourse to contract terms and gives AERB statutory status; draft rules were out for comment from 14 Aug to 4 Sep 2026.

name: Westinghouse AP1000 project at Kovvada, Andhra Pradesh
source: PIB parliament reply, Department of Atomic Energy (2 Apr 2026)
claim: DAE told Parliament on 2 Apr 2026 that supplier-recourse and section 46 provisions of the 2010 liability law delayed commercial agreements for Kovvada, designated for cooperation with the US, and that the SHANTI Act now aligns liability with international norms; no contract has been signed. The six-unit AP1000 plan (about 6,600 MW) comes from earlier project reports.

name: Holtec 10 CFR 810 authorisation for SMR technology transfer to India
claim: DOE authorised Holtec International in March 2025 under 10 CFR Part 810 to transfer unclassified SMR-300 technology to Holtec Asia, Larsen & Toubro and Tata Consulting Engineers, with state entities such as NPCIL and NTPC excluded pending Indian non-proliferation assurances. The authorisation text and date are not confirmed in the source.

name: India Nuclear Energy Mission (100 GW by 2047)
source: PIB parliament reply (23 Jul 2026); PIB press note (19 Dec 2025)
claim: The mission targets 100 GW by 2047 and at least five indigenous SMRs by 2033, with Rs 20,000 crore (about US$227m at Rs 88/US$) for SMRs. The roadmap takes capacity from 8.78 GW to about 22 GW by 2031-32 and NPCIL to about 54 GW, with the other 46 GW from other public companies, states, private firms and joint ventures.

name: Indian state refiners' LPG import contract from the US Gulf Coast for 2026
source: Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
claim: Indian state refiners concluded a one-year contract for about 2.2 Mt of US Gulf Coast LPG for 2026, around 10% of India's annual LPG imports, priced off Mont Belvieu. The volume, date and pricing basis are not confirmed in the source.

name: US-India Investment Incentive Agreement enabling DFC operations (2022)
claim: India and the US signed an Investment Incentive Agreement in Tokyo on 23 May 2022, replacing the 1997 agreement so DFC can offer loans, equity, guarantees and insurance in India. The signing date and terms are not confirmed in the source.

name: US-EU Joint Statement: non-tariff and economic-security commitments (CBAM, CSRD/CSDDD, EUDR, auto standards, critical-mineral export restrictions)
source: European Commission DG Trade (Joint Statement text)
claim: The 21 Aug 2025 Joint Statement commits the sides to mutual recognition of auto standards (para 8), to address US concerns on the EU deforestation regulation (para 10), to further CBAM flexibilities including for US SMEs (para 11), to keep CSRD/CSDDD from unduly restricting trade (para 12), to act together against third-country critical-mineral export restrictions (para 14) and to align on economic security, investment screening and export controls (para 19). None of these commitments carries a deadline or target.

name: MFN-only US tariff treatment for EU unavailable natural resources, aircraft and generic pharmaceuticals
source: European Commission press releases IP/25/1973 and IP/26/1103
claim: From 1 Sep 2025, EU unavailable natural resources (such as cork), all aircraft and parts, and generic pharmaceuticals with their ingredients and precursors pay MFN tariffs only, outside the 15% all-in ceiling, and both sides agreed to work on extending the regime to other products. The Commission's 20 May 2026 release still describes these exclusions as in place and further tariff cuts as work to come.

name: US-EU steel and aluminium tariff-rate-quota and overcapacity ring-fencing talks
institution: European Commission DG Trade / USTR / US Commerce
source: European Commission press releases IP/25/1973 and IP/26/1103
claim: In Aug 2025 the EU and US said they intend to ring-fence their markets from steel and aluminium overcapacity, including through a tariff-rate-quota solution for EU exports of steel, aluminium and their derivatives (Joint Statement para 3). The Commission's 20 May 2026 release still lists steel overcapacity as continuing work and announces no quota, so EU metals remain under the Section 232 tariffs (see USDE-07).

name: EU Steel Regulation 2026/1384 replacing the steel safeguard (18.3 Mt quotas, 50% out-of-quota duty)
institution: European Commission DG Trade and Economic Security
source: European Commission IP/26/1484; DG Trade news of 30 Jul 2026
claim: Since 1 Jul 2026 the EU has applied duty-free quotas of 18.3 Mt a year (an average 47% cut), a 50% out-of-quota duty on 26 steel categories and a melt-and-pour traceability rule. Half the quota is reserved for EU FTA partners, and the US has no FTA with the EU. Quota allocations run under a six-month urgency implementing act to be re-adopted before end-2026, and a product-scope review is due by 31 Dec 2026.

name: EU provisional safeguard on grain-oriented electrical steel, laminations and transformer cores
institution: European Commission DG Trade and Economic Security
claim: Provisional safeguard measures were imposed on 18 Sep 2026, after an investigation opened in March 2026. They cover GOES, laminations and cores, including cores already built into transformers, so they also shield EU transformer makers. Definitive measures need a qualified-majority vote, normally within nine months of the investigation opening (extendable to 11). Safeguards apply to imports of all origins, including the US; duty levels and country exclusions are not stated in the release.

name: Section 232 polysilicon proclamation: minimum import prices and 15% derivative tariff, with a 15% all-in cap for EU goods
technology: polysilicon; wafers; solar cells and modules
claim: The 6 Aug 2026 proclamation sets minimum import prices of US$21/kg for polysilicon, US$100/kg for ingots and wafers, US$0.22/W for cells and US$0.38/W for modules, plus a 15% duty on derivatives from 4 Dec 2026. For EU member-state products, MFN plus the Section 232 duty equals 15%, and drawback is allowed for goods made in Trade Agreement Partner countries, the EU included, when all their polysilicon also comes from such partners. Commerce and USTR may change MIP coverage for partners that adopt an equivalent MIP, and onshoring plans must start construction by 20 Jan 2029.

name: EU CBAM definitive regime from 1 Jan 2026 and the Joint Statement CBAM flexibilities
technology: steel; aluminium; hydrogen; fertilisers; cement; electricity
source: European Commission DG TAXUD CBAM pages
claim: Since 1 Jan 2026, EU importers of more than 50 tonnes a year of CBAM goods (iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity, hydrogen) must be authorised declarants. They surrender certificates priced at the quarterly average EU ETS auction price in 2026 (weekly from 2027), less any carbon price already paid abroad. The Joint Statement (para 11) commits the Commission to further flexibilities for US SMEs; the CBAM pages show no US-specific measure.

name: Revised EU Foreign Investment Screening Regulation (mandatory screening incl. critical raw materials)
institution: European Commission DG Trade and Economic Security
claim: Published on 26 Jun 2026, the regulation makes screening mandatory in every member state. It sets a minimum scope covering dual-use items, critical technologies, critical raw materials and energy, and extends to indirect investment and to EU firms controlled from outside the EU, so US investors are in scope. Member states have 18 months to apply it. The Joint Statement (para 19) commits the EU and US to cooperate on inbound and outbound investment reviews.

name: EU-US goods, services and investment volumes (2024-25)
source: European Commission DG Trade United States page; IP/26/1103
claim: EU-US goods trade was EUR 910.6bn in 2025, with an EU surplus of EUR 199.2bn. Services trade was EUR 865.2bn in 2024, with an EU deficit of EUR 178.4bn. Two-way investment stocks were EUR 4.8tn in 2024, and EU investment in the US employs 2.4m people.

name: EU energy imports from the US and the US$750bn purchase intent through 2028 (Commission breakdown)
claim: The Commission puts current EU imports of US LNG, oil and nuclear fuel and services at about US$90-100bn a year, against the US$750bn (about EUR 700bn) intent through 2028, or about US$250bn a year. The US supplied 55% of EU LNG in 2025 to date and 17% of 2024 oil imports, and US nuclear supplies were worth about EUR 700m in 2024. AggregateEU is to match EU buyers with US LNG for 2025-2050, but purchases remain commercial decisions.

name: EU LNG import capacity and US supply volumes
claim: EU LNG import capacity is about 250 bcm a year, more than double current LNG imports, after 12 new terminals and 6 expansions in 2022-24 added 70 bcm. The EU has imported about 50 bcm a year of US LNG in recent years, and 13 member states have LNG import infrastructure.

name: EU Methane Regulation importer requirements and October 2026 proposal to delay reporting
source: European Commission DG ENER methane emissions page
claim: Regulation (EU) 2024/1787, in force since 4 Aug 2024, phases in measurement, reporting and verification requirements for importers of oil, gas and coal. The Commission issued an importer guidance tool (Mar 2026, updated 22 Sep 2026) and a penalties recommendation (20 Jul 2026), then on 14 Oct 2026 proposed a one-year delay to the reporting provisions, citing Middle East supply pressure. The US supplies more than half of EU LNG (USEU-10), so most importer-side compliance falls on US supply chains.

name: Global Methane Pledge (EU-US launched 2021; US no longer co-convenor)
source: European Commission DG ENER methane emissions page
claim: The Commission and the US launched the pledge at COP26 in 2021 to cut methane emissions 30% by 2030. Canada replaced the US as co-convenor in 2025, and the Commission co-hosted the pledge ministerial at COP31 on 11 Nov 2026.

name: Venture Global-EnBW new mid-term LNG purchase agreements
claim: Binding agreements of 18 Jun 2026 add about 0.82 MTPA for about five years from 2026, supplied from Venture Global's portfolio, on top of EnBW's existing SPAs for 2 MTPA over 20 years.

name: Venture Global-Atlantic-SEE (AKTOR/DEPA Commercial) 20-year LNG SPA doubled to 1.0 MTPA
claim: Atlantic-SEE, an AKTOR-DEPA Commercial joint venture announced at the 6th Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation conference in Athens in Nov 2025, doubled its 20-year contract from 0.5 to 1.0 MTPA starting in 2030. Venture Global holds about 25% of the Alexandroupolis FSRU's regasification capacity, which feeds the Vertical Corridor to Central and Eastern Europe.

name: Venture Global-Naturgy 20-year LNG SPA (1 MTPA from 2030)
claim: Naturgy signed on 10 Nov 2025 for 1 MTPA over 20 years from 2030, Spain's first long-term US LNG contract since 2018. Venture Global had delivered 35 cargoes to Spain from Calcasieu Pass and Plaquemines.

name: Venture Global-Edison Calcasieu Pass arbitration settlement with extra cargoes for Italy
source: Venture Global / Edison joint press release
claim: The settlement signed on 26 Mar 2026 resolves Edison's whole Calcasieu Pass arbitration, with completion expected by end-Q2 2026. It also adds cargoes beyond the long-term contract, the first due in May 2026 at the Adriatic LNG terminal. Volumes and financial terms are not disclosed.

name: Venture Global-TotalEnergies mid-term LNG purchase agreement
claim: TotalEnergies agreed on 12 May 2026 to buy about 0.85 MTPA for about five years from 2026, supplied from Venture Global's portfolio. The destination market is not stated.

name: US-EU targeted critical minerals agreement negotiations (launched March 2023)
source: Joint Statement by President Biden and President von der Leyen (White House archive)
claim: On 10 Mar 2023 the leaders agreed to start negotiating a targeted agreement under which critical minerals extracted or processed in the EU would count toward the Section 30D clean-vehicle credit, building on the EU-US Task Force on the IRA. No agreement was concluded. The 30D credit ended for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, and the non-binding 24 Apr 2026 MOU (USDE-09) now carries the critical-minerals track.

name: CRMA second list: 46 new EU strategic projects; RESourceEU over EUR 2bn committed
institution: European Commission DG GROW / Critical Raw Materials Board
claim: On 9 Oct 2026 the Commission selected 46 strategic projects in 16 member states: 7 on lithium, 12 nickel, 10 cobalt, 5 manganese, 4 graphite and 4 rare earths. They add to 47 EU and 13 third-country projects chosen in 2025. Since the Dec 2025 RESourceEU communication, Team Europe has committed over EUR 2bn through the Innovation Fund, state aid and the EIB, and the Raw Materials Mechanism has made over 30 matches for 10 materials. No US company or US-located project is named.

name: Neo Performance Materials Narva (Estonia) rare-earth magnet plant in commercial production
claim: Neo, headquartered in Toronto with a US corporate office in Colorado, began commercial production at its Estonian plant in Sep 2026 and is shipping sintered magnets to a Tier 1 EV traction-motor customer. Phase 1A nameplate capacity is about 2,000 t/yr, and Phase 1B (about 5,000 t/yr) is in design. No US government role is stated; the company cites demand in Europe and North America.

name: EU Innovation Fund grant of up to EUR 126m for Neo's Project GAUSS and CRMA strategic-project status for Silmet 2.0
technology: rare earth separation, metals and magnets
source: Neo Performance Materials press releases (19 and 13 Oct 2026)
claim: On 19 Oct 2026 CINEA invited Neo to prepare a grant agreement of up to EUR 126m (about US$141m per the company) for Project GAUSS. The project would triple separation capacity at Sillamäe, add metallization and add up to 3,000 t/yr of magnets, a third earmarked for EU offshore wind. Silmet 2.0 was named on 9 Oct 2026 as the only rare-earth processing project in the CRMA's second strategic-project list.

name: Lyten acquisition of Northvolt Ett, Northvolt Labs and Northvolt Dwa (Sweden, Poland)
claim: US-based Lyten says it acquired the Northvolt Ett cell plant (Skellefteå), the Northvolt Labs R&D centre (Västerås) and the Northvolt Dwa BESS plant (Gdańsk) in the year to July 2026, and that it manufactures in Sweden and Poland. Prices, restart volumes and GWh are not disclosed. Lyten reports letters of intent for up to US$650m of US EXIM financing and over US$625m of equity, including from the European Investment Fund.

name: Lyten exclusive MOU to acquire Northvolt Drei (Heide) gigafactory assets
claim: On 1 Jul 2026 Lyten signed an exclusive MOU with KfW, Northvolt Drei Project GmbH and its shareholder LG Batterie GmbH for the 110-hectare Heide site, and an exclusivity agreement with Schleswig-Holstein. Lyten funds site preservation and targeted a definitive sale agreement in Q3 2026. Whether that agreement was signed is not stated in the source.

name: Westinghouse-Bechtel and PEJ Engineering Development Agreement for Poland's first nuclear plant
institution: Westinghouse / Bechtel / Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe / US DOE
claim: The EDA was signed in Warsaw on 28 Apr 2025, witnessed by Prime Minister Tusk and US Energy Secretary Wright. It covers site development, regulatory documents and geology for the three-unit AP1000 plant at Choczewo and runs until an EPC contract, then targeted for end-2025. Wright linked it to the US-Poland intergovernmental agreement begun in Trump's first term.

name: Westinghouse-Bechtel and PEJ agree main EPC commercial terms for three AP1000 units in Pomerania
claim: On 23 Sep 2026 the Westinghouse-Bechtel consortium and state-owned PEJ agreed the main commercial terms of the EPC contract for the three-unit AP1000 plant and aim to settle the remaining terms by end-2026. The EPC contract itself is not yet signed, and its value is not disclosed.

name: Westinghouse conditional purchase orders with four Polish module suppliers (Lubiatowo-Kopalino Unit 1)
claim: On 13 Oct 2026 Westinghouse placed conditional orders with EPG, FAMAK, Mostostal Kielce and Mostostal Krakow for the CA02, CA03, CA05 and CA20 modules of Unit 1. Each supplier gets its full scope once it reaches NQA-1 certification and passes mock-up qualification.

name: Westinghouse first Bulgarian purchase order for the Kozloduy AP1000 units
claim: On 7 Aug 2025 Westinghouse signed its first purchase order with MTG-Dolphin AD for the two-unit AP1000 expansion at Kozloduy. It covers an NQA-1 programme and engineering for a CA structural-module mock-up, and Westinghouse had MoUs with 29 Bulgarian suppliers. EPC contract and financing status are not stated in the source.

name: Westinghouse AP1000 FEED study at Jaslovské Bohunice, Slovakia, part-funded by US State Department FIRST grant
institution: Westinghouse / US Department of State / JESS
claim: Westinghouse launched a six-month FEED study on 28 Oct 2026 for one AP1000 unit, working for JESS, a subsidiary of state-owned JAVYS. The study is partly funded by a State Department FIRST programme grant and run under the Slovak-US intergovernmental agreement. The grant amount is not stated.

name: Fortum-Westinghouse early works agreement for a possible AP1000 in Finland
claim: Fortum signed an Early Works Agreement with Westinghouse, teamed with Hyundai E&C, on 23 Jun 2025 after a two-year feasibility study. It covers early planning, site evaluation and licensing work for a possible AP1000. No investment decision or site is stated.

name: LG Energy Solution North American ESS capacity expansion (Q3 2026 results)
claim: LGES's Q3 2026 results (3 Nov 2026) include KRW 416.9bn of North American production incentive. The company completed a new ESS line in Arizona, is expanding pack output in phases in Ohio and has restarted its GM joint-venture plant. It plans to lift North American ESS capacity to over 70 GWh by end-2027 by converting EV pouch lines, and to use four or more non-PFE LFP cathode suppliers in North America. Plant-level investment amounts are not stated.

name: Hanwha Defense USA takes controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard
institution: Hanwha Defense USA / Hanwha Systems / Hanwha Ocean
claim: On 29 Oct 2026 Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) said it is acquiring a controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard to turn it into a dual-use yard for naval and commercial work. In September Hanwha Systems agreed to sell its 60% stake to an HDUSA-led joint venture with Hanwha FutureProof; Hanwha Ocean holds the other 40%. The price and closing date are not stated.

name: Korea-US Shipbuilding Partnership Initiative (KUSPI) MOU and Shipbuilding Partnership Center
claim: MOTIR and the US Commerce Department signed the KUSPI MOU on 8 May 2026 and opened the Korea-US Shipbuilding Partnership Center in Washington on 23 Jul 2026, with Minister Kim and Secretary Lutnick attending. The center is meant to link governments, shipyards, research institutes and investors, train US shipbuilding workers, advise US yards on productivity and support joint R&D; 15 company and institution MOUs were signed at the opening.

name: Team Korea plan for APR1400 and AP1000 supply in the US (Nuclear Export Planning Committee)
claim: On 1 Oct 2026 MOTIR held its public-private Nuclear Export Planning Committee, set up in August 2026 with KEPCO, KHNP, KEPCO E&C, KEPCO Nuclear Fuel, KEXIM, K-SURE, builders and suppliers. It planned design, licensing, EPC and commissioning for the two APR1400 units under the Korea-US Nuclear Power Framework, and Korean supply into the six AP1000 units. US buyers were invited to supply-chain sessions at NES 2026 in Gyeongju on 27-29 Oct 2026.

name: Joint Ministerial Statement on Addressing Structural Excess Capacity and Production (sectoral platforms)
technology: EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors, solar panels
source: USTR press release and Joint Ministerial Statement text
claim: On 7 Oct 2026 the trade ministers of Argentina, Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Poland, Turkiye, the UK and the US signed a statement committing to new sectoral platforms on structural excess capacity. The platforms start with autos and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels, and officials are to meet at technical level before December 2026 to draft terms of reference and share data.

name: EFA and National Reconstruction Fund conditional finance for Astron Donald Mineral Sands rare earths project (framework one-year package)
institution: Export Finance Australia; National Reconstruction Fund Corporation
source: Export Finance Australia joint ministerial media release
claim: On 27 Oct 2026, a year after the US-Australia critical minerals framework was signed, EFA conditionally approved up to A$70m and the National Reconstruction Fund conditionally approved A$110m for Astron's Donald Mineral Sands Project in Victoria, a new source of light and heavy rare earths. The total is A$180m, about US$126m at US$0.70 per A$, and the form of the NRF investment is not stated. Ministers said more than A$6bn of support for critical-minerals projects had been announced since the October 2025 signing.

name: EFA conditional loan to Global Advanced Metals for tantalum production
source: Export Finance Australia joint ministerial media release
claim: On 27 Oct 2026, as part of a package marking one year of the US-Australia critical minerals framework, EFA conditionally approved a US$41.4m loan to Global Advanced Metals to support its tantalum production. Tantalum is used in electronic capacitors, aerospace alloys and medical implants.

name: Arafura binding NdPr offtake with a US trading group in Project Vault
institution: Arafura Rare Earths; unnamed US trading group (Project Vault participant)
source: Arafura Rare Earths quarterly activities report to 30 Sep 2026 (ASX)
claim: After 30 Sep 2026, Arafura signed a binding five-year offtake for Nolans NdPr with a US trading group named as a Project Vault participant, with volumes rising to 850 t/yr once the project reaches nameplate production. Arafura no longer names offtake counterparties and expects its remaining uncommitted NdPr to come from the 500 t/yr earmarked under Australia's Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve. The exact signing date is not stated in the report.

name: Sunrise Energy Metals Syerston scandium project final investment decision
institution: Sunrise Energy Metals; DoW Office of Strategic Capital
source: Sunrise Energy Metals ASX announcement headline (ASX platform); company investor presentation Sep 2026
claim: On 1 Nov 2026 Sunrise Energy Metals announced to the ASX that the board had approved a final investment decision for the Syerston scandium project in New South Wales, where early site works had already started. The project holds a DoW Office of Strategic Capital conditional loan commitment of up to US$400m. The FID funding terms, and whether the OSC loan was finalised at FID, are not stated in the headline.

name: Section 232 polysilicon action: minimum import prices and 15% duty on derivatives
institution: White House; Department of Commerce; CBP
source: White House proclamation 'Adjusting Imports of Polysilicon and its Derivatives into the United States'
claim: The proclamation of 6 Aug 2026 sets minimum import prices of US$21/kg for polysilicon, US$100/kg for ingots and wafers, US$0.22/W for cells and US$0.38/W for modules, with a specific tariff covering any shortfall. It also adds a 15% ad valorem duty on ingots and other derivatives. Both measures apply from 4 Dec 2026. For Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and EU members, the Section 232 duty plus the MFN rate equals 15%; for the UK the Section 232 rate is 10%. Partners that adopt a substantially equivalent minimum-price regime may receive different treatment.

name: Section 232 polysilicon onshoring programme and partner-polysilicon drawback
source: White House proclamation 'Adjusting Imports of Polysilicon and its Derivatives into the United States'
claim: Commerce may approve company onshoring plans for US polysilicon, ingot, wafer and cell plants whose construction starts by 20 Jan 2029. Approved companies may import equipment and covered products free of Section 232 duty, in volumes tied to the investment, and lose the benefit if they fail to perform. Manufacturing drawback is allowed for goods from Trade Agreement Partners (UK, EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Mexico, Canada) whose polysilicon comes entirely from partner countries and that are not subject to AD/CVD orders.

name: Commerce anti-stockpiling limits on polysilicon-chain imports before Section 232 duties
institution: Department of Commerce (BIS; Office of Strategic Industries and Economic Security); CBP
claim: In Sep 2026 Commerce barred established importers from bringing in volumes substantially greater than their historic averages before the 4 Dec 2026 duties. The averages are measured over 2025, 1 Jan to 6 Aug 2026, and the period since 6 Aug. Importers registered on or after 6 Aug are capped at 12 kg of polysilicon, 7 kg of wafers, 2,000 loose cells and 55 cells in modules. The Federal Register citation is not given in the source.

name: Section 201 safeguard on solar cells and modules expired (Feb 2026)
claim: The Section 201 safeguard tariff on solar cells and modules, imposed in President Trump's first term, expired in February 2026. The 6 Aug 2026 polysilicon proclamation states that its 15% duty on derivatives replaces this 'similar but narrower' safeguard. The exact expiry day is not stated in the source.

name: US antidumping orders on solar cells and modules from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam
technology: c-Si cells, whether or not assembled into modules
claim: The AD orders apply from 24 Jun 2025, after the ITC found material injury from Malaysia and Vietnam and threat of injury from Cambodia and Thailand (letter of 9 Jun 2025). Margins: Cambodia 125.37%. Malaysia 0% for Hanwha Q Cells Malaysia and 8.59% for Jinko and all others. Thailand 111.45% for Trina (202.90% for adverse-facts exporters). Vietnam 62.31% for JA Solar, 126.18% for Jinko, 85.45% for other named exporters and 271.28% Vietnam-wide.

name: US countervailing duty orders on solar cells and modules from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam
technology: c-Si cells, whether or not assembled into modules
claim: The CVD orders apply from 24 Jun 2025. Cambodia: 534.67% for all others (3,403.96% adverse-facts rate). Malaysia: 14.64% for Hanwha Q Cells Malaysia, 40.50% for Jinko and 34.09% for all others. Thailand: 255.39% for Trina and all others. Vietnam: 230.66% for Boviet, 68.15% for JA Solar and 124.57% for all others.

name: US antidumping orders on solar cells and modules from India, Indonesia and Laos
technology: c-Si cells, whether or not assembled into modules
claim: The AD orders apply from 9 Nov 2026, after the ITC's final material-injury determination of 2 Nov 2026 (701-TA-772-774, 731-TA-1756-1758). India: 123.04% (cash deposit 107.17%) for Mundra Solar PV, Mundra Solar Energy, Premier Energies, Kowa and all others. Indonesia: 94.36% for PT Blue Sky Solar, PT REC Solar Energy Indonesia and all others. Laos: 65.76% (deposit 65.36%) for Solarspace, including sales via JA Solar Vietnam and Trina entities, and for the Laos-wide entity.

name: US countervailing duty orders on solar cells and modules from India, Indonesia and Laos
technology: c-Si cells, whether or not assembled into modules
claim: The CVD orders apply from 9 Nov 2026. India: 126.09% for Mundra Solar Energy, Mundra Solar PV and all others, based on adverse facts. Indonesia: 73.20% for PT REC Solar Energy Indonesia and all others, and 173.70% for PT Blue Sky Solar. Laos: 82.03% for Solarspace and all others, and 153.67% for Vietnam Sunergy. The investigations were initiated by notices published 12 Aug 2025.

name: Commerce circumvention inquiry on Chinese solar cells completed in Ethiopia (and modules assembled in Vietnam)
claim: Commerce opened a country-wide circumvention inquiry, applicable 17 Jul 2026. It covers cells completed in Ethiopia from Chinese parts, and modules assembled in Vietnam from such cells, as possible circumvention of the AD/CVD orders on Chinese cells. The request was filed on 12 May 2026 by First Solar, Hanwha Q CELLS USA, Talon PV, Swift Solar, Great Lakes Solex PR, DYCM Power, Suniva and Silfab Solar. No preliminary determination is listed in the Federal Register's 2026 ITA index as of 13 Nov 2026.

name: UFLPA Entity List: polysilicon and solar-silicon firms
institution: DHS Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force; CBP
source: DHS UFLPA Entity List page (last updated 10/28/2026)
claim: The list has named Hoshine Silicon and Xinjiang Daqo New Energy since 21 Jun 2022. On 15 Jan 2025 it added Hongyuan Green Energy (Hoyuan, formerly Wuxi Shangji), Hongyuan New Materials (Baotou), Baotou Meike Silicon Energy, Jiangsu Meike Solar and Donghai JA Solar. On 3 Aug 2026 it added Xinjiang Goens Energy Technology (formerly Xinjiang GCL New Energy Material Technology) and TBEA Co. Goods from listed entities fall under the UFLPA import presumption.

name: UFLPA detentions of solar imports (Qcells, VSUN, Maxeon)
source: PV Tech (articles of Aug 2025, Mar 2026 and Apr 2026)
claim: Hanwha cells were reportedly detained in Aug 2025, and Qcells had resumed normal production at its Georgia module plants by 9 Mar 2026. CBP detained modules from Vietnam-based VSUN in Apr 2026, which could cut about US$30m from the company's earnings. CBP denied Maxeon's protests in Apr 2025; Maxeon's H1 2025 shipments fell to 153.2 MW (15% of H1 2024), and it applied for judicial management in Singapore in Apr 2026.

name: IRS Notice 2026-15: interim safe harbours for prohibited-foreign-entity (FEOC) rules under 45X, 45Y and 48E
claim: The OBBBA (P.L. 119-21, 4 Jul 2025) denies the 45X, 45Y and 48E credits to components and facilities that receive material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity. Notice 2026-15 sets interim safe harbours for computing the material-assistance cost ratio until proposed regulations are issued; the statute requires safe-harbour tables by 31 Dec 2026. The statute, not the notice, sets the solar-component threshold at 50% for 2026 sales, rising to 85% after 2029.

name: EU Net-Zero Industry Act: resilience criteria in auctions, procurement and support schemes
technology: solar PV and other net-zero technologies
claim: Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 sets a goal for EU net-zero manufacturing to meet at least 40% of annual deployment needs by 2030. Non-price criteria, including resilience, are mandatory in public procurement, in support schemes such as rooftop-PV subsidies, and in renewable auctions covering at least 30% of each member state's annual auctioned volume or 6 GW. Implementing acts in force from 18 Jun 2025 specify the criteria and the components that trigger the resilience test, based on a Commission dependency communication of 23 May 2025.

name: EU supply shares for PV products by third country (NZIA data for 2025)
source: Commission 'Preliminary informal shares of Union supply 2026'
claim: The Commission's preliminary data on 2025 shares of EU supply, used for the NZIA resilience criterion, are as follows. PV modules and cells: 95% from China. PV wafers: 59% China, 11% United States, 11% Singapore. PV inverters: 66% China, 8% Japan, 3% UK. Complete PV systems: 93% China, 2% Japan.

name: EU Forced Labour Regulation
source: European Commission Forced Labour Single Portal
claim: The regulation was adopted on 19 Nov 2024 and bans products made with forced labour from being sold in or exported from the EU market from 14 Dec 2027. A preparedness package, Single Portal, guidelines and a risk database were launched on 30 Jun 2026.

name: India ALMM List-II for solar PV cells
institution: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE)
claim: MNRE implemented ALMM List-II (approved solar cells) on 1 Jun 2026. Its 12th revision on 8 Oct 2026 brought enlisted cell capacity to 37.8 GW, against more than 217 GW of module capacity on List-I in Aug 2026. The exemption for net-metering and open-access projects runs to end-Dec 2026, and Wood Mackenzie expects List-II to cause cell shortages and higher system prices.

name: Chinese polysilicon producers' price floors and consolidation
institution: Chinese polysilicon producers (Tongwei, GCL and others)
claim: At a closed-door meeting in Hangzhou on 11 Oct 2026, producers agreed capacity self-control, floors of RMB43,000/t (about US$6,425/t) for polysilicon and RMB0.79/W (TOPCon) and RMB0.86/W (BC) for modules, and mutual supervision; the floors also apply to export and procurement bids. In Aug 2026 eight producers (Tongwei, GCL-Tech, Daqo, Xinte, Asia-Silicon, East Hope, Qinghai Lihao, Xinjiang Geensi) pledged not to sell below cost. Tongwei is negotiating to acquire Qinghai Lihao.

name: China proposed export controls on polysilicon, wafer and cell technologies
technology: polysilicon, wafer, cell and tandem production technology and equipment
source: PV Tech (citing MOFCOM announcement of 16 Oct 2026)
claim: On 16 Oct 2026 MOFCOM opened consultation on adding 12 PV technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, with temporary pre-export registration. The list covers fluidised-bed polysilicon processes (trichlorosilane lines of at least 250,000 t/yr; silane lines of at least 20,000 t/yr), technology for wafers 70 micrometres or thinner, cell edge passivation, and perovskite and tandem module production, including the associated equipment.

name: Drinda (Jietai) cancels 10 GW TOPCon cell plant in Oman
institution: Drinda New Energy Technology / Jietai Solar; Oman Investment Agency
source: PV Tech (citing Drinda board decision of 12 Nov 2026)
claim: Drinda dropped its planned 10 GW (two 5 GW phases) TOPCon cell plant in Sohar Free Zone, a project of about US$280m on which construction had not started. It cited trade and tariff shifts, Middle East uncertainty, slow local supply-chain development and China's proposed Oct 2026 PV technology export controls. It is redirecting HK$962.77m (US$122.7m) of proceeds, including HK$288.83m for silver paste and wafer procurement.

name: Meyer Burger collapse and sale of US HJT assets to Swift Solar
claim: Meyer Burger ended module production in Goodyear, Arizona in May 2025. Its two German subsidiaries, including the operator of the Thalheim cell plant, became insolvent in Jun 2025, and the group entered a debt moratorium in Sep 2025. In Mar 2026 Swift Solar bought its heterojunction patents and US manufacturing assets; other US equipment had gone to Waaree Solar Americas and Babacomari Solar North. The deal value is not disclosed.

name: REC Silicon closes Moses Lake solar-grade polysilicon plant
source: PV Tech ('The PV Review, 2025' and related articles)
claim: In early 2025 REC Silicon stopped solar-grade polysilicon production at Moses Lake, Washington, then the only operating US solar-grade site, after reported purity failures put its supply deal with Hanwha Qcells in doubt. Hanwha lent it US$40m for the shutdown and offered US$88.8m to buy the company in Apr 2025. Minority shareholders triggered an investigation in Jun 2025.

name: Highland Materials planned 20,000 t polysilicon plant, Tennessee
claim: Highland Materials plans 20,000 t/yr of polysilicon capacity in Tennessee. It has secured US$255m in tax credits, leased a former nuclear site, and says construction will start in H2 2026. Whether construction has begun is not stated in the source.

name: Wacker polysilicon earnings fall on solar-grade weakness
claim: Wacker reported lower polysilicon sales and earnings in Q1 2026 and a significant decline in polysilicon earnings in its Jul 2026 results, citing weak solar-grade business. PV Tech notes that Wacker and Hemlock, the legacy Western producers, have not expanded capacity in a decade.

name: US solar manufacturing capacity and production by stage (2026)
claim: US module capacity is 77.3 GW (61 GW crystalline), with 51.5 GW of production (37.5 GW crystalline). Cell capacity is 26.5 GW including thin film but only 10 GW crystalline, with 5.2 GW crystalline output. Wafer capacity is 5 GW with 3.2 GW produced. Polysilicon capacity is 36 GW against 15.5 GW of PV-allocated production. More than 40 GW of extra cell capacity is due within 18 months, and wafering is the tightest bottleneck.

name: Corning Michigan solar wafer plant and Arizona module plant
claim: Corning brought wafer production online at its Michigan plant in Q3 2025, targeting one million wafers a day. In Jul 2025 it bought JA Solar's 2 GW module assembly plant in Arizona. Its solar segment sales rose 37% year on year to US$436m in Q3 2026. In Oct 2026 First Solar sued JA and Corning's subsidiary American Panel Solutions over TOPCon patents.

name: Corning US polysilicon and wafer supply deals with T1 Energy, Suniva and Heliene
claim: In Mar 2025 Suniva, Heliene and Corning announced US-made modules with 66% domestic components. In Aug 2025 T1 Energy agreed to buy US-made polysilicon and wafers from Corning for its US cell production. Volumes and prices are not stated in the source.

name: ES Foundry PERC cell plant, Greenwood, South Carolina
claim: ES Foundry began PERC cell production at its 3 GW nameplate plant in Greenwood, South Carolina in Jan 2025 and completed a 2 GW expansion line there in Jul 2026. It plans a move to n-type cells. Total current capacity is not stated in the source.

name: NorSun 5 GW ingot and wafer plant plan, Tulsa, Oklahoma
claim: NorSun closed its 1 GW ingot and wafer plant in Norway in Dec 2024 to focus on a planned 5 GW plant in Tulsa, Oklahoma (announced Jun 2024). In Aug 2024 it agreed to supply US-made wafers to Heliene's planned 1 GW US cell plant from 2026. Construction status of the Tulsa plant is not stated in the source.

name: US solar cover-glass supply gap and new domestic glass lines
institution: Stewart Glass; Heliene; Illuminate USA; Solarcycle
claim: PV Tech describes domestic solar glass as a key gap in the US PV chain. Stewart Glass is adding a line at its Ohio solar-glass plant, expected in 2027 (announced May 2026). Heliene is trialling a new American-made solar glass (Aug 2026), and Illuminate USA signed a five-year deal in Aug 2025 to buy US-made glass from recycler Solarcycle.

name: Waaree solar glass plant, India
claim: Waaree Energies is developing an INR39bn (about US$415m, the source's conversion) solar-glass plant in India and has raised its holding in Kotsons. Capacity and start date are not stated in the source summary.

name: ReNew polysilicon and metallurgical-silicon investment, Andhra Pradesh
claim: ReNew plans US$1.2bn for polysilicon and metallurgical-silicon manufacturing in Andhra Pradesh, within an INR800bn (US$8.53bn) state investment covering solar manufacturing and a data centre. Capacity and timing are not stated in the source summary.

name: IEA: China's share of solar PV manufacturing stages
source: IEA, Solar PV Global Supply Chains (2022), executive summary
claim: China's share of every PV manufacturing stage exceeds 80% and was heading to almost 95% for polysilicon, ingots and wafers; Xinjiang alone held about 40% of global polysilicon output. Costs in China were 10% below India, 20% below the US and 35% below Europe, and electricity is over 40% of polysilicon production cost.

name: IEA Renewables 2025: PV supply-chain concentration and manufacturer losses
claim: The IEA expects concentration of key PV production segments to stay above 90% in 2030, even as capacity outside China grows. Chinese PV prices are down over 60% since 2023, cutting margins of the largest manufacturers to about -10%, with cumulative losses near US$5bn since early 2024.

name: Quad Clean Energy Supply Chain Principles and Diversification Program (Hiroshima)
source: White House fact sheet, Quad Leaders' Summit (20 May 2023)
claim: Quad leaders committed to identify and address gaps in manufacturing capacity for clean-energy technologies, focusing on solar PV, hydrogen electrolysers and EV batteries. They adopted joint principles for clean-energy supply chains and planned a public-private Quad Clean Energy Supply Chain Conference.

name: Quad Clean Energy Supply Chains Diversification Program funding (Wilmington)
source: White House fact sheet, 2024 Quad Leaders' Summit
claim: Australia was to open applications in Nov 2024 for the AUD 50m (about US$34m at Sep 2024 rates) programme supporting solar-panel, electrolyser and battery supply-chain projects in the Indo-Pacific. India committed US$2m to solar projects in Fiji, Comoros, Madagascar and Seychelles, and Japan US$122m to renewable projects. Awards and 2025-26 activity are not stated.

name: DFC loan to Tata Power Solar cell plant, India
institution: US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC); Tata Power Solar
source: White House fact sheet, 2024 Quad Leaders' Summit
claim: DFC extended a US$250m loan to Tata Power Solar to build a solar-cell manufacturing plant in India, reported as a US Quad contribution. Plant capacity and disbursement are not stated in the source.

name: DFC loan to First Solar module plant, India
institution: US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC); First Solar
source: White House fact sheet, 2024 Quad Leaders' Summit
claim: DFC extended a US$500m loan to First Solar to build and operate a solar-module manufacturing plant in India, reported as a US Quad contribution. Capacity is not stated in the source.

name: US withdrawal from the International Solar Alliance and IRENA
source: Presidential memorandum 'Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions, and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States'
claim: A presidential memorandum of 7 Jan 2026 directs US withdrawal from a list of organisations that includes the International Solar Alliance and the International Renewable Energy Agency.

name: EU-India Free Trade Agreement (concluded, awaiting signature)
institution: European Commission (DG TRADE); Government of India
claim: The EU and India concluded FTA negotiations on 27 Jan 2026. The deal eliminates or reduces tariffs on over 96% of EU goods exports to India. On 11 Sep 2026 the Commission sent proposals to the Council for signature and conclusion; investment-protection and GI agreements are still under negotiation. Solar-specific tariff lines are not described on the page.

name: EU-India Trade and Technology Council (third meeting)
source: European Commission EU-India agreements page (press release list)
claim: The EU and India held the third TTC meeting in Brussels on 15 Jul 2026, reaffirming the TTC as the central platform for cooperation on trade, technology and security. Clean-energy deliverables of the meeting are not described on the page.

name: US Section 301 tariffs on Chinese lithium-ion batteries, battery parts and natural graphite
technology: Li-ion batteries; battery parts; natural graphite
claim: Under the 2024 Section 301 four-year review, tariffs on Chinese lithium-ion EV batteries and battery parts rose from 7.5% to 25% in 2024, on non-EV lithium-ion batteries from 7.5% to 25% in 2026, and on natural graphite and permanent magnets from zero to 25% in 2026; certain other critical minerals went to 25% in 2024.

name: AD/CVD case on active anode material (graphite) from China ends without orders
source: Energy-Storage.news, 17 Mar 2026 (citing the USITC release of 12 Mar 2026)
claim: Commerce found dumping margins of 93.5% (July 2025) and, in February 2026, countervailing duties of 66.8% on Chinese active anode material, about 220% combined. On 12 Mar 2026 the USITC found the imports had not materially retarded the establishment of a US industry, so no AD/CVD orders issue and cash deposits are refunded (Inv. 701-TA-752 and 731-TA-1730). The case had been brought in December 2024 by the American Active Anode Material Producers coalition.

name: OBBBA prohibited-foreign-entity (FEOC) rules for 45X battery components and 48E energy storage
technology: Li-ion cells; battery components; energy storage
source: IRS One Big Beautiful Bill provisions page; IRS Notice 2026-15
claim: P.L. 119-21 (4 Jul 2025) makes components that include material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity ineligible for 45X in tax years beginning after enactment. It also denies 48E to energy storage whose construction begins after 31 Dec 2025 if the storage includes such assistance, and IRS Notice 2026-15 sets interim safe harbours for computing the material-assistance cost ratio. The statutory ratio thresholds rise each year: for qualifying battery components from 60% in 2026 to 85% from 2030, and for storage from 55% to 75%. The notice does not restate these thresholds.

name: China export controls on lithium-battery, cathode and artificial-graphite anode items (MOFCOM Oct 2025) and their one-year suspension
technology: Li-ion cells; LFP cathode; artificial graphite anode; production equipment
source: White House fact sheet, 1 Nov 2025 (suspension); scope of the 9 Oct measures from press coverage
claim: MOFCOM's 9 Oct 2025 package included controls, due to take effect on 8 Nov 2025, on high-energy-density lithium-ion cells, LFP and precursor cathode materials, artificial-graphite anode materials and related equipment and technology. After the Busan meeting China suspended the 9 Oct measures for one year, to about 10 Nov 2026.
