On 9 Nov 2026 MOFCOM/GAC Announcement 2026 No. 58 kept the battery and graphite-anode controls suspended to 10 Jan 2027 (CCRM-01).

name: China general licences for graphite and other critical-mineral exports to US end users (Busan deal)
technology: graphite; rare earths; gallium; germanium; antimony
claim: The White House says China will suspend the global implementation of the export controls it announced on 9 Oct 2025. It also says China will issue general licences for exports of rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite to US end users and their suppliers worldwide, which it calls the de facto removal of controls China has imposed since 2023.

name: DRC cobalt export ban replaced by export quotas (ARECOMS)
source: Le Monde, 25 Sep 2025 (headline); volumes from press coverage
claim: The DRC suspended cobalt exports on 22 Feb 2025 and replaced the ban with ARECOMS-allocated quotas from 16 Oct 2025. The quotas were reported as 18,125 t for the rest of 2025 and 96,600 t a year for 2026 and 2027, with part held back as a strategic quota. These volumes come from press reports, not the ARECOMS decision.

name: EVelution Energy-EGC-Trafigura MOU on Congolese cobalt hydroxide for a US refinery
institution: EVelution Energy; Entreprise Generale du Cobalt (EGC); Trafigura
source: Wikipedia (Mining industry of the DRC), citing Reuters and Bloomberg, 13 May 2026
claim: On 13 May 2026, US-based EVelution Energy signed an MOU with DRC state-owned EGC and Trafigura for a long-term supply of Congolese cobalt hydroxide to the refinery EVelution is building in the United States. The parties will also discuss an EGC minority stake in EVelution and more processing in the DRC. Volumes and refinery capacity are not stated.

name: Glencore MOU with the US-backed Orion Critical Mineral Consortium on DRC copper-cobalt assets
institution: Glencore; Orion Critical Mineral Consortium; US State Department
source: US State Department, 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial release
claim: Deputy Secretary Landau witnessed an MOU between Glencore and the US-backed Orion Critical Mineral Consortium on a potential acquisition of assets in the DRC. State says the deal reflects the US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement's aim of copper and cobalt flows to the United States. The assets, stake and price are not named.

name: US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement (mining investment and copper-cobalt supply)
institution: US State Department; Government of the DRC
source: US State Department, 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial release (refers to the agreement)
claim: The US and the DRC signed a Strategic Partnership Agreement alongside the December 2025 Washington peace accords. The State Department says its core objectives are more US investment in DRC mining and secure copper and cobalt flows to the United States. The text, any list of assets offered and the exact signing date (reported as 4 Dec 2025) are not confirmed in a primary source.

name: Indonesia nickel ore export ban
claim: Indonesia has banned nickel ore exports since January 2020 to force domestic smelting, after a 2014 ban was relaxed in 2017. The ban drew a wave of foreign investment into nickel and cobalt processing, and Indonesia produced about 1.6 Mt of the world's 3.3 Mt of nickel in 2022. Cobalt by-product output reached 20,500 t in 2024. The 2026 mining-quota (RKAB) cuts and royalty changes are not covered by this source.

name: US-Indonesia Agreement on Reciprocal Trade framework: removal of critical-mineral export restrictions to the US
institution: White House / USTR; Government of Indonesia
claim: Under the joint statement, Indonesia will remove restrictions on exports to the United States of industrial commodities, including critical minerals, and eliminate about 99% of tariff barriers on US goods. The US set a 19% reciprocal tariff on Indonesia, an IEEPA rate that was later struck down in February 2026. The statement does not say whether a final agreement was signed or how the nickel ore ban is treated.

name: EU Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 obligations and timelines
source: European Commission DG Environment batteries page; dates from press coverage
claim: The regulation sets binding sustainability, safety, labelling, supply-chain due-diligence and end-of-life rules for portable, LMT, EV, industrial and SLI batteries. Due-diligence obligations were postponed from August 2025 to 18 Aug 2027, and the battery passport applies from 18 Feb 2027. The Commission page does not restate these two dates.

name: RESourceEU finance and the EU Raw Materials Mechanism (demand aggregation and offtake matching)
claim: Since the RESourceEU communication of December 2025, Team Europe has committed more than EUR 2bn (about US$2.3bn at 1.16 USD/EUR) through the Innovation Fund, State aid and the EIB. The Raw Materials Mechanism, which aggregates demand and matches offtakers, has produced more than 30 matches for 10 materials. Of the 2025 Strategic Projects, 25 have completed environmental assessment and 17 hold construction permits.

name: Chile: Codelco-SQM lithium joint venture Nova Andino Litio formed (Salar de Atacama)
claim: Nova Andino Litio, the public-private joint venture that merges SQM's Salar de Atacama lithium operation with a Codelco subsidiary, was formed in December 2025 under an agreement that runs to 2060. Chile's Supreme Court rejected Tianqi Lithium's legal objection in late January 2026.

name: DOE loan office (EDF, formerly LPO) restructures the Biden-era loan portfolio
institution: DOE Office of Energy Dominance Financing
source: DOE EDF, Letter from Leadership: 2025 Year-in-Review, 22 Jan 2026
claim: DOE says it is restructuring, substantially revising or eliminating more than US$83.6bn of the US$104bn in Biden-era loans and conditional commitments: US$29.9bn de-obligated and US$53.6bn revised. Its priorities are now nuclear, hydrocarbons, critical minerals, geothermal, grid and manufacturing. The letter does not list which battery loans (BlueOval SK, StarPlus, Ultium Cells and others) were changed.

name: BlueOval SK: US$9.63bn DOE loan and dissolution of the Ford-SK On joint venture
source: Wikipedia (BlueOval SK), citing DOE, Ford and Kentucky press
claim: DOE closed a US$9.63bn direct loan to the joint venture in December 2024. In December 2025 Ford and SK On agreed to dissolve it: a Ford subsidiary takes the Kentucky plants, to be retooled for grid and data-centre storage, and SK On takes Tennessee. The Kentucky workforce was laid off by February 2026, with about 2,100 rehires planned in 2027, and Kentucky lawmakers questioned the state's US$250m forgivable loan. How the DOE loan was treated after the split is not stated.

name: Ford terminates about US$6.5bn of LG Energy Solution EV battery supply contracts for Europe
source: CNBC, 17 Dec 2025 (citing an LGES regulatory filing)
claim: On 17 Dec 2025 LGES disclosed that Ford had ended two contracts, signed in October 2024, to supply EV batteries for Ford in Europe from 2026 and 2027, worth about US$6.5bn. The termination followed Ford's decision to halt some EV models and its announced US$19.5bn writedown.

name: Tesla-LG Energy Solution US$4.3bn LFP storage-cell supply from Michigan
source: Ars Technica, 30 Jul 2025 (citing Korea Economic Daily and Reuters)
claim: Tesla agreed to buy about US$4.3bn of LFP cells from LGES's Michigan plant, most likely for its energy-storage products. The contract runs to at least the end of July 2030 with extension provisions and reduces Tesla's reliance on CATL. The counterparty was identified through press reports.

name: Northvolt bankruptcy and Lyten acquisition of its Swedish and Polish plants
claim: Northvolt filed for US Chapter 11 on 21 Nov 2024 with US$5.8bn of debt and for Swedish bankruptcy on 12 Mar 2025. During 2025 US-based Lyten bought most of its assets, including the Skelleftea gigafactory, a Polish storage plant and the intellectual property, and rehired staff to prepare a restart. EXIM issued Lyten a letter of interest for up to US$650m for a planned Nevada plant.

name: Verkor Dunkirk gigafactory ramp-up
claim: Verkor inaugurated its Dunkirk gigafactory in late 2025 and said in March 2026 that it had entered the final ramp-up phase. In August 2026 it commissioned a second production line and delivered the first batteries made entirely on site. Its target is 16 GWh a year of cell capacity.

name: Syrah Vidalia natural-graphite active anode material plant (Louisiana)
claim: Syrah's 11.25 ktpa Vidalia plant began AAM production in February 2024 from Balama (Mozambique) graphite. It is backed by a US$102m DOE loan (binding July 2022), a Tesla offtake (December 2021), a Lucid offtake (February 2025) and a US$165m 48C credit (January 2025). The credit supports a 45 ktpa expansion whose FID depends on financing. Syrah describes itself as the only operating vertically integrated natural-graphite AAM supplier outside China.

name: NOVONIX Chattanooga synthetic graphite: mass-production qualification sample to Panasonic
claim: On 11 Jun 2026 NOVONIX delivered a mass-production qualification (C-) sample of synthetic graphite AAM from Chattanooga to its lead customer Panasonic Energy; the company calls it the first such sample made in North America. It expects mass production for Panasonic in H2 2027, subject to qualification. The release does not mention the status of its DOE conditional loan.

name: Redwood Materials-GM/Ultium Cells recycling and second-life storage partnership
institution: Redwood Materials; General Motors; Ultium Cells
claim: Redwood has received more than 28,000 t of material for recycling from GM and Ultium Cells (GM's joint venture with LG Energy Solution), and about 10,000 GM EV packs are in the pipeline for repurposing through Redwood Energy. Its second-life system in Sparks, Nevada serves AI firm Crusoe, and a 1.5 MW/7.2 MWh repurposed-pack installation is planned at a GM plant in Michigan.

name: Hanjung America ESS plant, Huntington, Indiana, supplying StarPlus Energy
institution: Hanjung America (Hanjung NCS); StarPlus Energy (Samsung SDI-Stellantis)
claim: Hanjung America, a subsidiary of Korea's Hanjung NCS, announced its first ESS manufacturing plant in Huntington, Indiana to support StarPlus Energy. StarPlus's Kokomo plant will make NCA and later LFP ESS cells under Samsung SDI's KRW1.5tn (about US$1bn) four-year US supply deal. Investment and capacity are not stated.

name: Lobito Corridor partnership (US, EU, Angola, DRC, Zambia)
institution: US (PGI) / European Commission (Global Gateway) / Angola / DRC / Zambia
claim: In October 2023 the EU and the US signed an MOU with Angola, the DRC and Zambia to develop the Lobito rail corridor from the Copperbelt to the Atlantic, backed by a EUR 116m Global Gateway package and US PGI funding. The first DRC copper reached the US via Lobito in August 2024. In November 2025 China signed a US$1.4bn upgrade of the competing TAZARA line with Zambia and Tanzania. This source does not confirm the size or status of the US DFC loan to the railway concessionaire.

name: US bilateral critical-minerals frameworks signed at the February 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial; FORGE replaces the MSP
source: US State Department, 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial release
claim: At the 4 Feb 2026 ministerial (54 countries and the European Commission), the US signed 11 bilateral critical-minerals frameworks or MOUs: Argentina, Cook Islands, Ecuador, Guinea, Morocco, Paraguay, Peru, the Philippines, the UAE, the UK and Uzbekistan. These add to 10 signed in the previous five months, with negotiations concluded with 17 more countries; the frameworks cover pricing, development, supply gaps and access to finance. FORGE, chaired by Korea through June 2026, replaced the Minerals Security Partnership.

name: EXIM Project Vault: up to US$10bn direct loan for a US critical-minerals reserve
institution: Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM)
source: US State Department, 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial release
claim: The EXIM board approved a direct loan of up to US$10bn for Project Vault, a domestic strategic reserve for critical minerals meant to shield manufacturers from supply shocks; this is more than double EXIM's previous largest financing. EXIM has also issued US$14.8bn in letters of interest for critical-minerals projects under the current administration. Which battery minerals the reserve holds is not stated.

name: EU strategic partnerships on raw materials (17 partner memoranda)
source: European Commission, Raw materials diplomacy page
claim: The EU has raw-materials partnership memoranda with 17 partners. They include Argentina (13 Jun 2023), Chile (18 Jul 2023), the DRC and Zambia (26 Oct 2023), Norway (21 Mar 2024), Australia (28 May 2024), Canada (2021), South Africa (20 Nov 2025), the United States (24 Apr 2026) and New Caledonia (20 Oct 2026). They rest on letters of intent or political frameworks, with no binding volumes or finance.

name: EU-Chile Interim Trade Agreement in force; Advanced Framework Agreement in ratification
institution: European Commission (DG Trade); Government of Chile
source: European Commission DG Trade, EU-Chile page
claim: The EU-Chile ITA, signed on 13 Dec 2023, entered into force on 1 Feb 2025; the AFA, which adds investment protection, awaits ratification by all member states. The Commission links the agreement to Global Gateway work on lithium and copper value chains and green hydrogen in Chile. The EU is Chile's largest source of FDI, with a stock of EUR 57bn in 2024.

name: SK On cuts US EV-cell workforce in Georgia and Tennessee
claim: SK On took sole ownership of the Tennessee plant when the BlueOval SK joint venture was dissolved in December 2025. In March 2026 it laid off more than a third of the workforce at its Commerce, Georgia EV-cell plant, and 150 employees at the Tennessee site were laid off the same month.

name: China extends suspension of its October 2025 export controls to 10 Jan 2027 (MOFCOM/GAC Announcement 2026 No. 58)
technology: rare earths; superhard materials; lithium-battery and graphite-anode materials
claim: Announcement 2026 No. 58 of 9 Nov 2026 keeps MOFCOM/GAC Announcements 2025 Nos. 55, 56, 57 and 58 and MOFCOM Announcements 2025 Nos. 61 and 62 suspended from 11 Nov 2026 to 10 Jan 2027. These are the October 2025 controls on superhard materials, rare-earth equipment, further medium and heavy rare earths, lithium-battery and graphite-anode items, the extraterritorial rare-earth rule and rare-earth technology. The extension adds two months to the Busan-truce suspension, which was due to lapse on 10 Nov 2026. China's April 2025 licensing of seven medium and heavy rare earths (UJ-024) is not part of the suspension.

name: China's suspension of the gallium, germanium and antimony export ban on the US (to 27 Nov 2026)
technology: gallium; germanium; antimony; superhard materials; graphite
source: Xinhua via english.gov.cn / China Daily (MOFCOM statement)
claim: On 9 Nov 2025 MOFCOM suspended clause 2 of Announcement No. 46 of 2024 until 27 Nov 2026. That clause barred, in principle, exports to the US of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard-material dual-use items, and subjected graphite exports to stricter end-user and end-use checks; licensing still applies. No extension of this suspension was reported as of 13 Nov 2026.

name: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: refining concentration and exposure to Chinese export controls
source: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 (executive summary)
claim: Excluding rare earths, the top refining country's average share of key energy minerals rose to 72% in 2025 from 70% in 2023. China is the top refiner of each key energy mineral except nickel, where Indonesia leads. The number of mineral tariff codes under Chinese export controls has tripled since 2023. Full implementation of the expanded rare-earth controls could put about US$6.5 trillion a year of downstream production outside China at risk; a full disruption of battery-grade graphite trade would put over US$300bn a year at risk.

name: China's share of global copper smelting capacity reaches 50% (IEA 2026)
source: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 (executive summary)
claim: China's share of global copper smelting capacity rose from about 15% to 50% by 2025. China accounted for over 90% of the growth in global smelting capacity since 2005. Benchmark copper smelter treatment charges settled at US$0 per tonne for 2026. The IEA's projected 2035 copper supply deficit narrowed from about 30% to 25%.

name: China's share of battery recycling capacity (IEA 2026)
source: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 (executive summary)
claim: China holds over three-quarters of global battery-recycling pre-treatment capacity and 90% of material-recovery capacity. Recycling's share of key energy-mineral supply could rise from about 10% today to close to 20% by 2040.

name: China's share of rare-earth refining falls to about 85% (IEA 2026)
source: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026; Reuters report (via search summary)
claim: New refining projects in the US and Malaysia cut China's share of rare-earth refining to about 85% in 2025 from 90% in 2023; it could fall to about 70% by 2035 if all planned projects proceed (IEA figures as reported by Reuters). The executive summary adds that diversified refining capacity by 2035 equals about two-thirds of expected mined supply, while planned magnet production equals only about one-third. Diversifying magnet rare-earth supply would need about US$60bn of investment over a decade.

name: Price gaps between Chinese and non-Chinese critical minerals (IEA 2026)
source: IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 (executive summary)
claim: Between January 2025 and April 2026, lithium prices more than doubled, cobalt rose about 130% and tungsten rose sixfold. In Europe, gallium, dysprosium and terbium cost about five times Chinese domestic prices, and germanium almost three times. Refining outside the dominant supplier costs 20% to over 150% more in capital and about 50% more to operate. The net annual cost of stockpiling 11 high-risk materials outside the dominant supplier is under US$900m.

name: EXIM direct loan of up to US$10bn to Project Vault (US Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve)
institution: Export-Import Bank of the United States
claim: On 2 Feb 2026 EXIM's board approved a direct loan of up to US$10bn to Project Vault, an independently governed public-private partnership that will build the US Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve in facilities across the US. OEMs indicating participation include Clarios, GE Vernova, Western Digital and Boeing; the suppliers are Hartree Partners, Mercuria Americas and Traxys. The release does not name the minerals, the loan tenor or the private capital amount.

name: Project Vault becomes operational with US$1bn from Glencore and Mercuria
claim: VaultCo said on 23 Sep 2026 that Swiss-based traders Glencore and Mercuria had each committed US$500m, and the reserve moved into its operating phase. It is separate from the DLA-run National Defense Stockpile. No mineral purchases, EXIM loan closing, purchase-pricing rules or price-floor mechanism had been disclosed by mid-October 2026. The reported scope is the 60-mineral USGS list, with initial emphasis on rare earths, cobalt, nickel, lithium, copper, gallium, germanium and scandium.

name: Section 232 proclamation on processed critical minerals and derivative products (negotiations, price floors)
claim: The 14 Jan 2026 Section 232 proclamation imposes no tariffs. It directs Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements with trading partners and to promote price floors for trade in processed critical minerals and derivative products. Further import measures may follow if agreements are not reached within 180 days (about 13 Jul 2026), are not carried out or prove ineffective. The fact sheet cites no import-dependence figures.

name: Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals (ATCM): USTR-led plurilateral price-floor negotiations
source: Climate Leadership Council (citing USTR releases and Reuters)
claim: USTR is negotiating a binding plurilateral ATCM. Japan, Mexico and the EU are the first partners, building on action plans of 4 Feb, 19 Mar and 24 Apr 2026, and the design envisages phased-in, mineral-specific, border-adjusted price floors with common standards. As of 28 Sep 2026 no text was public, a reported initial scope of 5-10 minerals was unconfirmed and US implementing legislation would be needed. G7 trade ministers endorsed plurilateral agreements on 5-6 May 2026, and a Feb 2026 USTR comment request drew about 2,500 comments.

name: US-EU Action Plan for Critical Minerals Supply Chain Resilience
claim: Announced on 24 Apr 2026 as the primary US-EU mechanism for coordinating trade measures on critical-minerals supply chains, 'with a view to concluding a binding plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals'. The parties will examine tools including border-adjusted price floors; the release names no minerals, price levels or deadlines. The plan accompanies the State Department-Commission MOU of the same day (USDE-09).

name: US-Malaysia MOU on diversifying critical minerals supply chains and promoting investment
claim: Signed in Kuala Lumpur on 26 Oct 2025, the non-binding MOU commits both sides to coordinate support for bilateral projects and to prioritise US investment in Malaysian critical-minerals assets offered for sale. It also commits them to strengthen review of rare-earth asset sales and to protect both markets through high-standard marketplaces under a pricing framework that includes price floors or similar measures. Working-level meetings are to be quarterly, and no funds are obligated.

name: US-Thailand MOU on diversifying critical minerals supply chains and promoting investment
claim: Signed in Kuala Lumpur on 26 Oct 2025, the MOU gives the Participants an expected first opportunity to invest in critical-minerals assets offered for sale in Thailand or by Thai companies. It provides for early sharing of tender information, US help in assessing Thailand's resource base, technology transfer, priority for domestic processing and national-security review of rare-earth asset sales. Both sides will trade preferentially in high-standard marketplaces under a pricing framework that includes price floors or similar measures.

name: Malaysia keeps its raw rare-earth export ban despite its US no-restriction commitment
claim: Under the 26 Oct 2025 US-Malaysia reciprocal trade agreement, Malaysia agreed not to ban or impose quotas on exports of critical minerals or rare earths to the US. On 29 Oct 2025 its trade minister said the January 2024 ban on raw rare-earth exports remains, so rare earths must be processed in Malaysia before export.

name: Feb 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial: bilateral frameworks (Argentina, UK, Mexico and others) and reference-price trade zone proposal
claim: The 4 Feb 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial at the State Department drew 55 foreign delegations and produced 13 bilateral critical-minerals frameworks or MOUs. These include a framework with Argentina, an agreement with the UK and a US-Mexico action plan proposing border-adjusted price floors, with details due within 60 days; the source does not name the other signatories. Vice President Vance proposed a plurilateral preferential trade zone with reference prices at each production stage, enforced by adjustable tariffs, and FORGE replaced the MSP.

name: Minerals Security Partnership Finance Network
institution: MSP partner ECAs and DFIs (DFC, EDC, JICA, JBIC, KEXIM, Eksfin and others)
source: Joint statement establishing the MSP Finance Network (reprint)
claim: A joint statement in New York on 23 Sep 2024 set up a network of MSP export-credit agencies, development-finance institutions and state-backed funds. Its purpose is to share information, coordinate and co-finance critical-minerals projects. Named members include DFC, Export Development Canada, JICA, JBIC, KEXIM and Export Finance Norway among others; the full membership list is not confirmed in the source.

name: G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance, first round (26 investments, C$6.4bn)
claim: Announced in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025, this is the first round of the Production Alliance under the June 2025 G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan. Its 26 investments, partnerships and measures with France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Norway, the US, Australia and Ukraine aim to unlock C$6.4bn (about US$4.6bn at 0.71 USD/CAD) of graphite, rare-earth and scandium projects. They include Government of Canada offtakes with Nouveau Monde Graphite and Rio Tinto (scandium) and up to C$20.2m for joint R&D. Canada also released a roadmap for standards-based critical-minerals markets.

name: G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance, second round (30 partnerships, C$12.1bn)
claim: At PDAC on 2 Mar 2026 Canada announced a second round of 30 partnerships and investments with 12 allied partners, covering C$12.1bn (about US$8.6bn at 0.71 USD/CAD) of projects. This brings the Alliance total to C$18.5bn of Canadian critical-minerals projects. The release does not name the partners or the projects.

name: Canada to stockpile critical minerals under the Defence Production Act and the Defence Industrial Strategy
source: Natural Resources Canada news releases (Oct 2025, Mar 2026)
claim: On 31 Oct 2025 Canada said it would use the Defence Production Act to stockpile critical minerals. The stated purposes are domestic and allied defence supply, Arctic sovereignty and NATO goals. The Defence Industrial Strategy of 17 Feb 2026 allows stockpiling of critical and dual-use minerals. Volumes and budget are not stated.

name: Canada Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund (C$2bn; reported renamed Canada Critical Minerals Accelerator)
claim: Budget 2025 (4 Nov 2025) created a C$2bn (about US$1.4bn) fund over five years from 2026-27, administered by Natural Resources Canada, to provide equity, loan guarantees and offtake. It was due to launch in spring 2026. A Fall 2026 law-firm primer says it was renamed the Canada Critical Minerals Accelerator, and no completed investment is confirmed.

name: IEA Critical Minerals Security Programme expanded (2026 Ministerial)
claim: At the 19 Feb 2026 Ministerial, IEA ministers endorsed an expanded phase of the Critical Minerals Security Programme, which was established in 2022. The expansion covers: support for members that set up or expand stockpiles; rapid market assessments and coordinated responses during supply disruptions; regular table-top exercises (a rare-earth exercise was held in Nov 2025); a wider information dashboard; a new Technology Collaboration Programme on recycling and substitution. The release gives no budget.

name: RESourceEU Action Plan (EUR 3bn, Critical Raw Materials Centre, joint purchasing, stockpiling)
claim: Adopted on 3 Dec 2025, the plan allocates EUR 3bn (about US$3.5bn at 1.16 USD/EUR) of EU funds over 12 months to projects that can provide alternative supply in the short term, and creates a European Critical Raw Materials Centre. It uses the Raw Materials Platform to aggregate demand, purchase jointly and secure offtakes, and it develops a coordinated EU approach to stockpiling. It aims to cut dependencies by up to 50% by 2029 and builds on 15 strategic partnerships.

name: India National Critical Mineral Mission
source: IEA policy database; Indian press (via search summary)
claim: India's Cabinet approved the mission on 29 Jan 2025 for 2024-25 to 2030-31, with INR 16,300 crore of public outlay (about US$1.9bn at INR 86.5) and a further INR 18,000 crore expected from public-sector undertakings and private firms. It covers exploration, overseas acquisition, processing parks and recycling.

name: India Rare Earth Permanent Magnet manufacturing scheme (INR 7,280 crore, 6,000 t/yr)
institution: Government of India (Ministry of Heavy Industries)
claim: India's Cabinet approved on 26 Nov 2025 an INR 7,280 crore scheme (about US$820m at INR 89) for 6,000 t a year of integrated rare-earth permanent-magnet capacity, covering oxide to metal, metal to alloy and alloy to magnet. It provides INR 6,450 crore of sales-linked incentives and INR 750 crore of capital subsidy, and it complements the National Critical Mineral Mission.

name: Korea public critical-minerals stockpile target (KOMIR, over 100 days by 2031)
institution: Korea Ministry of Trade / KOMIR / Public Procurement Service
claim: Korea's trade ministry plans to raise public stockpiles of 13 core minerals from about 51 days of supply to over 100 days by 2031. KOMIR holds the stockpiles with the Public Procurement Service. The 2023 critical-minerals strategy had set a 100-day target, and in Feb 2026 KOMIR set a target of a 20% critical-mineral recycling rate by 2030.

name: JOGMEC-Iwatani investment in Caremag (Carester) rare-earth recycling and refining plant, Lacq
source: Argus Media; Fastmarkets; METI joint release (via search summary)
claim: JOGMEC and Iwatani committed up to EUR 110m (about US$120m) of equity and shareholder debt through Japan France Rare Earths Company; the French state provides EUR 106m, for EUR 216m in total. The Lacq plant is designed to recycle 2,000 t of magnets and refine 5,000 t of concentrates a year, producing about 600 t a year of dysprosium and terbium oxides. Iwatani is to take about 250 t of Dy and 45 t of Tb a year, about 20% of Japan's projected heavy rare-earth demand. Operations are targeted for end-2026.

name: Lynas Malaysia first separated heavy rare earths outside China
source: Malay Mail; Mining Technology (via search summary)
claim: In May 2025 Lynas produced dysprosium oxide at its Malaysian plant, the first commercial separated heavy rare earth outside China, with terbium scheduled from June 2025. The new circuit can separate up to 1,500 t of heavy rare earths a year. Output volumes were not disclosed.

name: Neo Performance Materials sintered NdFeB magnet plant, Narva (Estonia)
claim: Neo opened the Narva plant on 19 Sep 2025 at sample-production stage. Phase 1 output of 2,000 t a year of sintered NdFeB magnets is targeted by Q2 2026, with later growth to 5,000 t. Reported investment is EUR 75-96m, and feedstock comes from Neo's Silmet separation plant in Sillamae, Estonia.

name: DOE equity warrants in Lithium Americas and the Thacker Pass JV (loan restructuring)
institution: US Department of Energy / Lithium Americas
source: Creamer Media; Lithium Americas release (via search summary)
claim: DOE restructured the US$2.23bn Thacker Pass loan (announced about 30 Sep 2025, finalised 8 Oct 2025). DOE receives penny warrants for a 5% equity stake in Lithium Americas and a 5% economic stake in the Thacker Pass JV, which Lithium Americas owns 62% and GM 38%. DOE also defers US$184m of debt service, and the company adds US$120m to reserve accounts. The warrants remain subject to definitive documents.

name: US government 10% equity stake in Trilogy Metals (Ambler district, Alaska)
institution: US government (reported as Department of War) / Trilogy Metals
claim: In October 2025 the US government agreed to take a 10% equity stake in Vancouver-based Trilogy Metals for about US$35.6m. The stake came with approval of the Ambler Road to Trilogy's copper-zinc-cobalt district in northwest Alaska. Reports attribute the stake to the Department of War; the closing terms are not stated in these sources.

name: Vulcan Elements and ReElement US$1.4bn partnership (OSC loans, Commerce equity, DoW warrants)
institution: Office of Strategic Capital / Commerce CHIPS Program Office / Vulcan Elements / ReElement
technology: NdFeB magnets; rare-earth separation and recycling
claim: The US$1.4bn package has four parts: a US$620m OSC direct loan to Vulcan Elements for a 10,000 t/yr magnet plant; an US$80m OSC loan to ReElement for separation and recycling; US$50m of CHIPS incentives from Commerce, taken as equity in Vulcan; Department of War warrants in both companies. Vulcan adds US$550m of private capital. The plant site was not named, and the loans were conditional on diligence when announced.

name: USA Rare Earth definitive CHIPS agreements with Commerce (up to US$1.6bn, about 10% stake)
institution: US Department of Commerce / USA Rare Earth
technology: NdFeB magnets; heavy rare-earth metal and alloy
claim: On 3 Jun 2026 USA Rare Earth signed definitive agreements with Commerce under the CHIPS programme for up to US$1.6bn: about US$277m of funding and a US$1.3bn senior secured loan, released against milestones. Commerce receives 16.1m shares and about 17.6m warrants, roughly 10%. The Stillwater, Oklahoma magnet line was commissioned in April 2026 and is expected to reach 600 t a year by end-2026. The company targets 10,000 t of magnets including a planned South Carolina site.

name: US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund
source: Government of Ukraine (Ministry of Economy release on kmu.gov.ua)
claim: The fund has US$150m of seed capital, US$75m each from DFC and Ukraine; the agreement entered into force on 23 May 2025. It has a board and investment, audit, administrative and prospecting committees, and Alvarez & Marsal was appointed investment adviser on 14 Nov 2025. Critical minerals is one of five priority sectors, and the indicative timeline targets the first three investment decisions by end-2026.

name: Dobra lithium deposit tender won by TechMet-backed JV
institution: Dobra Lithium Holdings (TechMet / The Rock Holdings) / Government of Ukraine
claim: Dobra Lithium Holdings, a JV of US government-backed TechMet and The Rock Holdings, won the tender for Ukraine's Dobra lithium deposit with a reported US$179m investment commitment. Reports differ on whether the award was in Nov 2025 or Jan 2026, and the proposal terms are not public. Dobra is not in the Reconstruction Investment Fund portfolio, whose first investment (March 2026) was in a drone-communications company.

name: US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement on minerals (Strategic Asset Reserve)
institution: US State Department / Government of the DRC
source: Rio Times; IEA policy database (via search summary)
claim: Signed on 4 Dec 2025 and tied to peace in eastern DRC, the agreement creates a Strategic Asset Reserve: a list of Congolese mining assets on which US companies get preferential access. The IEA summary adds a right of first offer on minerals marketed for export to US persons. The steering committee met on 5 Feb 2026, when the first asset list was designated, and in Paris on 5 Nov 2026. At the Paris meeting the SAR legal framework was still not final, and DFC presented DRC investments in preparation without figures.

name: USGS final 2025 List of Critical Minerals (60 minerals)
institution: US Geological Survey (Department of the Interior)
claim: The final 2025 list, published on 7 Nov 2025, has 60 minerals, up from 50 in 2022. It adds boron, copper, lead, metallurgical coal, phosphate, potash, rhenium, silicon, silver and uranium. The list is to be updated not less than every two years.

name: Section 232 copper tariff (50% on semi-finished products; refined copper phase-in undecided)
claim: Proclamation 10962 (30 Jul 2025) imposed a 50% tariff on the copper content of semi-finished copper products and intensive derivatives from 1 Aug 2025. It does not stack on Section 232 auto tariffs. A refined-copper duty of 15% from 1 Jan 2027 and 30% from 1 Jan 2028 depended on a Commerce market update due 30 Jun 2026, and no decision on it was reported.
